lessons.title: Strings, alphabets and languages
lessons.summary: An alphabet supplies symbols; a language selects finite strings over it.
lessons.body:
A simplified vending-machine controller can track bounded credit, and a simplified traffic light can track its current phase. Real controllers may also track timers, sensors and historical data. Both are **finite-state machines**: at any moment they are in one of a fixed, finite set of states, and each input moves them to another state.

A **deterministic finite automaton** (DFA) is the mathematical version of that idea, stripped down to its essentials. It reads a string one symbol at a time, changes state on each symbol, and at the end says yes or no. It is the simplest model of computation that is still useful, and it sits underneath lexers, regex engines, network protocol parsers and hardware controllers.

## Strings and languages

An **input alphabet** supplies the allowed symbols, such as the bits 0 and 1. A **string over an alphabet** is a finite sequence of those symbols: `0110` has four symbols. A **formal language** selects which strings count as valid. The **membership problem** asks whether one particular string belongs to that selection.

The **empty string** has no symbols. It is still a string: a language containing only it has one member, whereas the empty language has none. A language may contain finitely or infinitely many strings; each individual string remains finite.

The compact notation below is useful when reading later proofs. Its meaning is the same selection-of-strings idea:

```formula reference
Σ = {0, 1}   or   Σ = {a, b}
w = 0110   so   |w| = 4
|ε| = 0
Σ* = {ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, …}
L ⊆ Σ*
where
Σ: capital Greek sigma: the input alphabet, a finite set of symbols the machine can read
{ }: curly braces: the set containing exactly the items listed inside, in any order
a, b: two example symbols, used as the letters of an alphabet
w: an example string: a finite sequence of symbols from Σ, here the four symbols 0, 1, 1, 0 in that order
| |: vertical bars around a string mean its length: how many symbols it contains
ε: Greek epsilon: the empty string, the string with no symbols at all (in Python, "")
*: the Kleene star: Σ* is the set of every finite string you can build from the symbols of Σ, including ε. It is infinite for a non-empty alphabet; for the empty alphabet it contains only ε. Each string is finite
…: and so on without end
L: a formal language: any set of strings over Σ
⊆: is a subset of: every element of the left-hand set is also in the right-hand set
In words: an alphabet is a finite set of symbols; a string is a finite row of them (0110 has length 4, ε has length 0); Σ* collects every possible string; and a language is any collection of those strings, so it is a subset of Σ*.
```

"Binary strings with an even number of 1s" is a language. So is "valid Python identifiers" and "binary numbers divisible by 3". A DFA implements one such yes-or-no membership rule.

Some textbooks require an alphabet to be non-empty; if the empty alphabet is permitted, its only finite string is the empty string. Neither convention makes the empty language the same thing as the language containing only the empty string.

## Key takeaways
- An alphabet supplies symbols; a language selects finite strings over it.
- The empty string is a string of length zero, distinct from an empty language.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

options.explanation: Correct. A string is a sequence, whereas a language is a set of sequences. A set containing the empty string has one member.

2. Put that sequence into a set: the set now has one member.
3. Compare with a set containing no sequences: that is the empty language.
4. A language can therefore be empty, contain only the empty string, or contain other strings as well.

lessons.title: DFA states, transitions and runs
lessons.summary: A complete DFA specifies exactly one transition for every state and symbol.
lessons.body:
## What the machine needs to remember

A DFA carries one current state through the input. Each state summarises the past well enough to decide what to do with the next symbol. For even parity, it needs only "even so far" or "odd so far", not the entire string.

Its five ingredients are the finite set of **automaton states**, an **input alphabet**, a **transition function**, one **start state** and a set of **accepting states**. The transition function gives exactly one next state for every state and input symbol.

Begin each independent run in the start state. Read one symbol and follow its transition, then repeat. Test acceptance only after all input has been read. Visiting an accepting state midway does not end the run; later input can move elsewhere. On empty input, the start state itself decides.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A board-game counter
> A counter marks your current square; a drawn card tells you where to move next.
>
> **How it maps:** The square represents the current state and each card an input symbol. A fixed rule tells you the next square. The finishing square determines acceptance.
>
> **Where it stops:** A DFA has no dice or player choice, and its verdict is checked when the input ends, not as soon as it visits a special square.

## Reference notation

Mathematicians describe a DFA by listing its five ingredients in a fixed order, a 5-tuple. Any DFA, however big, is fully pinned down by these five things:

```formula reference
M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F)
δ : Q × Σ → Q
q₀ ∈ Q
F ⊆ Q
where
M: the machine, the DFA being described
( , , , , ): round brackets with commas: an ordered list of components (a tuple); here there are five, so it is a 5-tuple
Q: the finite set of automaton states
Σ: capital Greek sigma: the input alphabet, the finite set of symbols the DFA can read
δ: Greek delta: the transition function. δ(q, c) is the one state to move to from state q on reading symbol c
×: the Cartesian product: Q × Σ is the set of every (state, symbol) pair
→: maps to: δ takes a pair from the set on the left and returns one element of the set on the right
q₀: "q nought": the start state, where every run begins
∈: is an element of
F: the set of accepting states (also called final states)
⊆: is a subset of: every element of F is also in Q; F may be empty or all of Q
In words: a DFA has a finite set of states, an alphabet, a rule giving exactly one next state for every state and symbol, one start state, and a chosen set of accepting states.
```

For the even-parity machine in the next unit:

The parity states are E (even so far) and O (odd so far). Start in E. A 1 swaps states; a 0 leaves the state alone. Only E accepts.

The language of a DFA is the set of all strings whose complete runs end in accepting states.

For example, the even-parity machine reads 1011 and finishes in O (traced in the next parity-cycle unit). O is not accepting, so 1011 is not in the machine's language.

"Deterministic" means there is never a choice: for every state and every symbol there is exactly one move. So a DFA's run on a given string is a single path, and it takes exactly n steps for a string of length n.

## Key takeaways
- A complete DFA gives exactly one transition for every state and input symbol.
- A run applies that function once per symbol and tests the final state for acceptance.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

questions.prompt: A DFA with 50 states reads a 1,000,000-character string. Which describes the work it does?

options.text: About 50 × 1,000,000 steps, because it checks every state at each symbol
options.explanation: A DFA is in exactly one state at a time. It never examines the other 49. That "all states" picture describes NFA simulation, not DFA.

options.text: Exactly 1,000,000 transitions and memory that does not grow with the input
options.explanation: One transition per symbol, with a stored transition table and only one current state; auxiliary memory is independent of input length for this fixed machine.

options.text: It may need to backtrack, so the worst case is exponential
options.explanation: Determinism means there is never a choice to undo. Backtracking is a property of some regex engines, not of DFAs.

options.text: It must first store the whole string so it can check the end
options.explanation: A DFA reads left to right once and never looks back, so it needs no buffer.

questions.workedExample: The machine follows exactly one transition per input symbol. It stores only its current state during the run, regardless of input length. The transition table is stored separately and its size depends on the machine. No backtracking or whole-input buffer is required for membership.

lessons.title: Designing parity and length cycles
lessons.summary: Parity needs only the distinction between even and odd, rather than a full counter.
lessons.body:
The earlier definition specifies a start state, a set of accepting states and exactly one next state per symbol. Here E means an even number of 1s so far and O means an odd number; start and accept in E.

## Example 1: an even number of 1s

The language is binary strings with an even number of 1s. The only thing the machine needs to remember is the **parity** so far: even or odd. That is two states.

```
        0                0
       +-+              +-+
       v |              v |
 --> ((E)) ----1----> ( O )
         <----1------
```

The double brackets mark E as accepting. The arrow from nowhere marks it as the start. As a **transition table**, which is how you would store it in code:

| State | on 0 | on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| → E (accept) | E | O |
| O | O | E |

Trace `1011`:

```
start  E
  1 -> O
  0 -> O
  1 -> E
  1 -> O    end in O: reject
```

Three 1s is odd, so rejecting is right. Notice the DFA never counts the 1s. It only tracks the one bit of information that matters. Designing a DFA is mostly the art of asking "what is the least I need to remember?"

A four-state cycle can similarly track the input length modulo four: each input symbol advances one position, and only the starting position accepts. Four prefixes of lengths zero through three need distinct futures: append enough symbols to bring one chosen length to a multiple of four, and the others still have different remainders.

## Key takeaways
- Parity needs only the distinction between even and odd, rather than a full counter.
- A length-divisibility cycle stores a fixed remainder; distinguishable futures justify the state count.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

questions.prompt: The two-state DFA for "an even number of 1s" (start E, accepting E; a 1 swaps E and O, a 0 stays put) reads `110101`. Where does it finish, and does it accept?

options.text: Finishes in O, rejects
options.explanation: This would be right for an odd number of 1s. `110101` has four 1s, so the parity ends even.

options.text: Finishes in E, accepts
options.explanation: Correct. Each 1 toggles the state and each 0 leaves it alone. Four 1s means four toggles, which lands back on E.

options.text: Finishes in E, rejects
options.explanation: E is the accepting state, so finishing there means accept. This mixes up "ending state" with "accept/reject".

options.text: It cannot decide without counting all the 1s first
options.explanation: This DFA tracks parity directly. DFAs can count up to a fixed bound or modulo a constant; they cannot maintain an unbounded exact counter.

questions.workedExample:
Follow the transition function one symbol at a time:

```
start  E
  1 -> O
  1 -> E
  0 -> E
  1 -> O
  0 -> O
  1 -> E   accept
```

The string has four 1s. Each 1 flips the parity and 0s change nothing, so after an even number of flips we are back in E, which is accepting.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of states for a DFA over {a, b} that accepts exactly the strings whose length is a multiple of 4 (including the empty string)?

options.explanation: Two states cannot separate all four prefix classes. For example, suffixes completing a multiple of four distinguish ε, a, aa and aaa pairwise.
A fifth state is not needed. Length mod 4 has only four values, and a dead state never arises because every string can still reach a multiple of 4.
Correct. Track length mod 4 in a 4-cycle; state 0 is start and accepting. Fewer is impossible because ε, a, aa and aaa all need different futures.

options.text: It cannot be done with a DFA because it needs to count
options.explanation: It needs to count only modulo 4, which is bounded. Unbounded counting is what DFAs cannot do.

questions.workedExample:
1. What must we remember? Only the length mod 4: values 0, 1, 2, 3.
2. Build a cycle: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 0 on either a or b. Start and accept at 0.
3. Why not fewer? Take the empty string, a, aa and aaa. For any two of them, some suffix of a's makes exactly one of the two reach a multiple of 4. For example, appending aaaa to the empty string gives length 4 (accepted), but appending it to a gives length 5 (rejected). Four prefixes that must be kept apart need four states.

This "distinguishable prefixes" argument is the Myhill–Nerode idea from the minimisation units.

lessons.title: Recognising binary remainders
lessons.summary: Appending a bit doubles a binary value and adds the bit; remainders can be updated directly.
lessons.body:
## Remember the remainder, not the number

Read a binary number left to right, most significant bit first. Appending a bit to the right of a binary number doubles its value and adds the new bit, just as appending a digit in decimal multiplies by 10 and adds it. The machine cannot store the whole value, which grows without limit, but it does not need to: the remainder after dividing by 3 can be updated from the old remainder alone.

```formula essential
r′ = (2r + b) mod 3
where
r: the remainder of the binary prefix after division by three, initially zero
b: the next bit read, 0 or 1
r′: the new remainder, one of zero, one and two
mod: the remainder after whole-number division, so 7 mod 3 = 1 and 9 mod 3 = 0
In words: the new remainder depends only on the old remainder and the new bit, never on the full value. So three states, one per possible remainder (0, 1 or 2), are enough.
```

For example, after reading `100` the value is 4 and the remainder is 1. Reading a 1 doubles four and adds one, giving nine. Updating just the remainder doubles one and adds one, giving three and therefore remainder zero: the same answer, because nine is divisible by three. This works because multiples of 3 contribute nothing to a remainder after doubling, so they can be thrown away at every step.

| Remainder | on 0 | on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| → 0 (accept) | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | 0 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |

Trace `1001` using the table: the remainders are 0, 1, 2, 1, 0. The final remainder is zero, so the machine accepts. There is no need to convert the whole input to an integer first, even when it is too long to fit in a fixed-width integer.

And `101` (5) goes 0 → 1 → 2 → 2, ending in 2: reject. The same trick builds a DFA for "divisible by k" with k states, in any base.

> [!note] What about the empty string?
> This DFA accepts the empty string, because the start state is accepting. Whether the empty string "is divisible by 3" is a design decision. If you want to reject it, add a separate start state. Edge cases like this are where hand-built automata most often go wrong.

## Running a DFA in Python

A DFA is just a lookup table and a loop. This is the whole simulator:

```python
def run_dfa(delta, start, accept, w):
    # Reset each independent membership run.
    q = start
    for c in w:
        if (q, c) not in delta:
            return False   # no move: reject
        # Keep only the state for this
        # prefix.
        q = delta[(q, c)]
    # Acceptance is tested after all input.
    return q in accept

# Store only each prefix remainder.
D3 = {(r, b): (2 * r + int(b)) % 3
      for r in range(3) for b in "01"}

print(run_dfa(D3, 0, {0}, "1001"))  # True
print(run_dfa(D3, 0, {0}, "101"))   # False
```

The cost is O(n) time for a string of length n, for a fixed machine with O(1) transition lookup, using constant auxiliary state storage beyond the stored machine and input. That is the defining property of finite automata and the reason they are used for high-throughput scanning: they never need to look back, buffer or backtrack.

## Key takeaways
- Appending a bit doubles a binary value and adds the bit; remainders can be updated directly.
- The remainder construction gives a sufficient state count, which may shrink through equivalent states.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

questions.prompt: Two binary prefixes leave the same remainder after division by three. You append the same bit to each. What must happen to their remainders?

options.text: They must become different
options.explanation: Different full values do not matter once their remainders agree.

options.text: The machine must recover both original values
options.explanation: Multiples of three can be discarded before the update without changing the remainder.

options.text: Their new remainders are the same
options.explanation: Correct. Doubling each value and adding the same bit preserves agreement modulo three.

options.text: It depends on the preceding independent run
options.explanation: Each independent run starts afresh; the current prefix remainder summarises this run.

questions.workedExample: Appending a bit doubles the prefix value and adds that bit. Prefixes with the same remainder differ by a multiple of three. Doubling that difference still gives a multiple of three, so both updates produce the same remainder. This is why a remainder is sufficient state.

questions.prompt:
A complete DFA for binary values divisible by four starts and accepts in state 0, including empty input. Its remainder transitions are:

```
state  on 0  on 1
0      0     1
1      2     3
2      0     1
3      2     3
```

Which is the minimum state count after merging equivalent states?

options.explanation: Remainders 1 and 3 behave identically: both go to 2 on 0 and to 3 on 1, and neither accepts. So they can be merged.
Correct. Only the last two bits matter. States 1 and 3 merge (last bit was 1), leaving "accepting 0", "last bit 1" and "last bits 10".
There are three distinguishable situations: accepting remainder 0, remainder 2, and an odd remainder. The empty suffix separates 0 from the others; the suffix 0 separates 2 from an odd remainder.
No dead state is needed: any prefix can still become a multiple of 4 by appending 00.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write the transitions:

```
r  on 0      on 1
0  0         1
1  2         3
2  0         1
3  2         3
```

2. 1 and 3 are both non-accepting with identical rows, so no suffix can tell them apart: merge them.
3. 0 and 2 have identical rows too, but 0 accepts and 2 does not (try the empty suffix), so they stay separate.
4. Result: 3 states. The intuition: divisibility by 4 depends only on the last two bits, and "last bit 1" is one situation, whatever came before.

lessons.title: Partial DFAs and safe complementation
lessons.summary: A missing transition rejects through an implicit dead state.
lessons.body:
## Dead states and partial DFAs

Strictly, the transition function must be defined for every (state, symbol) pair: it must be **total**. A DFA where that holds is a **complete DFA**. In practice people draw **partial DFAs** and leave missing arrows implied. A missing arrow means "go to a **dead state**" (also called a trap or sink): a non-accepting state that loops to itself on every symbol. Once you fall in, you can never accept.

Here is a DFA for unsigned decimals such as `42` and `3.14`: one or more digits, optionally followed by a dot and one or more digits. `d` stands for an ASCII digit, 0 through 9.

| State | on d | on . |
|---|---|---|
| → S | WHOLE | dead |
| WHOLE (accept) | WHOLE | DOT |
| DOT | FRAC | dead |
| FRAC (accept) | FRAC | dead |

- `3.14`: S → WHOLE → DOT → FRAC → FRAC. Accept.
- `3.`: ends in DOT, which is not accepting. Reject.
- `.5`: S on `.` goes to dead. Reject.
- `1.2.3`: FRAC on `.` goes to dead. Reject.

This is exactly the regex `[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?`, and lexers for programming languages are built from automata like this one for every token type.

## Complementing safely

To recognise the complement over the same alphabet, first make all missing transitions explicit by adding a rejecting dead state that loops on every symbol. Then swap accepting and non-accepting states, including the dead state. For the decimal machine, `.5` must be accepted by the complement even though its first dot makes the original partial run stop.

## Key takeaways
- A missing transition rejects through an implicit dead state.
- Make the transition function total before swapping accepting status to form a complement.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

questions.prompt: You have a partial DFA for decimals (`[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?`) with no explicit dead state. To recognise the complement, you swap accepting and non-accepting states and do nothing else. Which input does the new machine get **wrong**?

options.explanation: The original accepts `3.14` and it ends in FRAC, which becomes non-accepting after the swap. The new machine rejects it, which is correct for the complement.
The original ends in DOT (non-accepting). After the swap DOT is accepting, so the new machine accepts `3.`, which is correct for the complement.
The original accepts `42` in WHOLE. After the swap WHOLE is non-accepting, so `42` is rejected, which is right.
Correct. `.5` falls off the partial DFA at the first symbol (no move from S on `.`), so it is rejected before and after the swap. The complement should accept it.

questions.workedExample:
1. A missing transition is an implicit dead state, and a run that hits it rejects.
2. Swapping the accepting states only touches the states that exist. The implicit dead state stays "reject".
3. So any string that fell off the original is rejected by both machines, yet the complement should accept it.
4. `.5` falls off at the first character.

Fix: add the dead state explicitly (every missing arrow goes to it, and it loops to itself), then swap. The dead state becomes accepting.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
D = {("S","d"):"I", ("I","d"):"I",
     ("I","."):"P", ("P","d"):"F",
     ("F","d"):"F"}

def run(w):
    q = "S"
    for c in w:
        digit = c in "0123456789"
        if not digit and c != ".":
            return False
        # Map ASCII digits to one label.
        k = "d" if digit else c
        q = D.get((q, k))
        # Missing transitions reject.
        if q is None:
            return False
    return q in {"I", "F"}

# A trailing dot leaves P non-accepting.
print([run(w) for w in
       ["0", "0.0", "00.", "1.23"]])
```

options.text: `[True, True, False, True]`
options.explanation: Correct. `0` ends in I, `0.0` and `1.23` end in F, and `00.` ends in P, which is not accepting.

options.text: `[True, True, True, True]`
options.explanation: This treats `00.` as valid, but after the dot the machine is in P, which needs at least one more digit before accepting.

options.text: `[True, False, False, True]`
options.explanation: `0.0` is fine: S→I on 0, I→P on the dot, P→F on 0, and F is accepting.

options.text: `[False, True, False, True]`
options.explanation: A single digit is a complete integer: S→I, and I is accepting.

questions.workedExample:
Trace each input:

```
"0"    S -d-> I            accept
"0.0"  S -> I -.-> P -> F  accept
"00."  S -> I -> I -.-> P  P not in F
"1.23" S -> I -> P -> F -> F accept
```

lessons.title: Combining DFAs with product states
lessons.summary: A product state records one state from each component.
lessons.body:
## Combining DFAs

Languages recognised by DFAs are called **regular languages**. They are closed under the usual operations on sets, and the proofs are constructions you can actually run.

### Complement

To recognise everything a complete DFA rejects, swap accepting and non-accepting states. The DFA for "odd number of 1s" is the earlier parity DFA with O accepting instead of E.

> [!warning] Complete the DFA first
> Swapping only works if the transition function is total. In a partial DFA, strings that "fall off" are rejected both before and after the swap. Add the dead state explicitly, then swap, and the dead state becomes accepting.

### Intersection and union: the product construction

Take two complete DFAs over the same alphabet. To recognise the strings both of them accept, run the two machines **in parallel**. A state of the product machine is a pair: where the first machine is, and where the second machine is. This is the **product construction**:

For intersection, accept only when both component states accept. For union, accept when either does. Both use the same pairs and transitions; changing the final test changes the combined language.

The notation records this construction for reference:

```formula reference
Q = Q₁ × Q₂
δ((p, q), c) = (δ₁(p, c), δ₂(q, c))
q₀ = (q₁, q₂)
F_{∩} = { (p, q) : p ∈ F₁ and q ∈ F₂ }
F_{∪} = { (p, q) : p ∈ F₁ or q ∈ F₂ }
where
Q₁, Q₂: the sets of states of the first machine M₁ and the second machine M₂
Q: the set of states of the product machine
×: the Cartesian product: Q₁ × Q₂ is the set of all pairs (p, q) with p from Q₁ and q from Q₂
p: a state of the first machine
q: a state of the second machine
( , ): an ordered pair: first component from M₁, second from M₂
c: one input symbol
δ₁, δ₂: the transition functions of the two machines
δ: the transition function of the product: it moves both components at once on the same symbol
q₁, q₂: the start states of the two machines
q₀: the start state of the product, the pair of the two start states
F₁, F₂: the accepting-collections of states of the two machines
F_{∩}: the accepting states for intersection (strings both machines accept)
F_{∪}: the accepting states for union (strings at least one machine accepts)
∈: is an element of
{ (p, q) : … }: the set of all pairs that make the condition after the colon true
In words: the product machine tracks both machines at once. It moves each one on every symbol, and it accepts according to a rule: both accept for intersection, at least one accepts for union.
```

Pairing the two parity states with the three remainder states gives six possible pairs. Only reachable pairs need to be built, and equivalent pairs may merge later. The product size is an upper bound on the necessary machine, not a claim of minimality.

For the intersection, `1001` is accepted: it has an even number of 1s and represents nine, divisible by three. A pair with even parity but nonzero remainder fails the intersection and passes the union. Acceptance still happens only after the whole input.

Because the sizes multiply, intersecting k machines multiplies all k of their sizes together. This blow-up is real and shows up in model checking and in regex engines that support intersection.

## Key takeaways
- A product state records one state from each component.
- Intersection requires both components to accept; union requires at least one.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)

questions.prompt: You combine two complete DFAs over the same alphabet to accept only strings both accept. What must a product state record?

options.text: Only whether either machine currently accepts
options.explanation: That loses the states needed to process future input.

options.text: The current state of each component
options.explanation: Correct. A pair retains both machines’ progress and moves both on the next symbol.

lessons.title: Finite memory: uses and limits
lessons.summary: Counters restricted to a finite range and fixed nesting limits can be represented by finitely many states.
lessons.body:
A DFA has finitely many states and one transition per input symbol. In the cost discussion below, n is the input length in symbols. Any fixed finite language can be recognised by a trie of its strings plus a rejecting dead state.

## Where DFAs are used

- **Lexers.** Tools such as lex and flex compile token patterns to automata. One DFA membership scan is linear; longest-match tokenization, backup, rescanning and actions need separate complexity analysis.
- **Regex engines** such as RE2 and Rust's regex can combine DFA and NFA strategies; supported searches have input-linear bounds for a fixed pattern. GNU grep also uses other strategies depending on pattern and mode. The practical regex units cover this.
- **Protocols and parsers.** HTTP parsers, UTF-8 validators and network packet filters are frequently hand-written state machines.
- **Hardware.** A synchronous digital circuit with bounded discrete internal state can be modelled as a finite-state machine; this abstraction omits analog timing effects. Controllers are designed as state diagrams and then synthesised.
- **Game AI and UI flows.** Enemy behaviour (patrol, chase, attack) and multi-step forms are often modelled as state machines, though these usually carry extra data so they are not pure DFAs.

## What a DFA cannot do

A DFA has a fixed number of states, so it can only remember a bounded amount of information. It cannot count without limit. "Equal numbers of a's and b's" or "balanced brackets" need unbounded memory, and no DFA recognises them. The pumping-lemma units prove this claim. A fixed bound changes the problem: matching brackets to depth three needs states for the four possible depths and a dead state for an invalid prefix.

That limitation is also the strength: because memory is bounded, a fixed-machine membership scan of a string of length n takes O(n) transitions and O(1) auxiliary space (a constant amount, however long the input), and many questions about DFAs (is the language empty? are two DFAs equivalent?) are decidable and fast. For more powerful machines those same questions become hard or impossible.

## Key takeaways
- Counters restricted to a finite range and fixed nesting limits can be represented by finitely many states.
- Unbounded matching counts and unrestricted balanced brackets need more memory than a DFA supplies.

## Further reading
- [MIT: finite automata and regular expressions](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/lecture-1-introduction-finite-automata-regular-expressions/)

questions.prompt: Which of these languages are regular, meaning some DFA recognises them? Select all that apply.

options.text: Binary strings with an even number of 0s
options.explanation: Regular: two states for the parity of 0s.

options.text: Strings over {a, b} with equally many a's and b's
options.explanation: Not regular. The machine would need to remember the difference between the counts, which is unbounded, so no finite set of states suffices.

options.text: Binary numbers divisible by 7
options.explanation: Regular: the remainder construction gives 7 states, one per value of v mod 7.

options.text: Strings over {a, b} in which, for every prefix, the number of a's minus the number of b's stays between −2 and 2
options.explanation: Regular. The difference is bounded, so five states (−2 to 2) plus a dead state track it exactly.

options.text: Balanced bracket strings like `(()())` with any bracket nesting depth
options.explanation: Not regular. Unbounded depth needs an unbounded counter. You need a stack (a pushdown automaton).

questions.workedExample:
Ask "how much must the machine remember?"

| Language | Memory needed | Regular? |
|---|---|---|
| even 0s | 1 bit | yes |
| equal a and b counts | unbounded count | no |
| divisible by 7 | 7 values | yes |
| difference −2 to 2 | 5 values plus a dead state | yes |
| balanced, any depth | unbounded depth | no |

The trap is the fourth: it looks like counting, but the count is bounded, and bounded counting is fine for a DFA.

questions.prompt: Which consequences follow from using a fixed finite-state DFA? Select all that apply. In the options, n is the input length or the stated count of repeated symbols.

options.text: Membership takes O(n) time for a string of length n
options.explanation: True. One transition per symbol, never more.

options.text: The memory used while running does not grow with the input
options.explanation: True. Only the current state is stored.

options.text: Some DFA accepts exactly n a’s followed by n b’s when n ranges from zero to one million
options.explanation: True, surprisingly. The language is finite, and every finite language is regular. The DFA is enormous (millions of states), but it exists.

options.text: Some DFA accepts exactly n a’s followed by n b’s for every non-negative count n
options.explanation: False. With no bound on n, the machine would need to remember an unbounded count of a's. The pumping-lemma units proves no DFA can.

questions.workedExample:
1. Time and space follow straight from the definition: one state, one lookup per symbol.
2. Finite languages: build a trie of all the strings; it is a DFA with at most (the sum of the string lengths, plus 1) states, plus a dead state.
3. For n a's then n b's with a cap of 1,000,000, the DFA counts a's up to the cap and then counts b's down. Over two million states, but finite.
4. Remove the cap and any fixed number of states, say k, fails: after reading more than k a's, two different counts must share a state (pigeonhole), and the machine can no longer tell how many b's to expect.

questions.prompt: A bracket validator accepts exactly balanced strings of ( and ) with bracket nesting depth at most 3, such as (()(())), and rejects strings that exceed that depth. How many states does a minimal complete DFA need?

options.explanation: Depths 0 to 3 give four states, but a complete DFA also needs somewhere to go on a `)` at depth 0 or a fourth `(`.
Correct. States for depth 0, 1, 2, 3 (start and accept at 0), plus one dead state for a closing bracket at depth 0 or exceeding depth 3.
This might come from two cubed, but the machine tracks a single depth number, not a set of three independent bits.

options.text: Impossible: bracket matching is not regular
options.explanation: Unbounded nesting is not regular. With a cap on the depth, the counter is bounded, so a DFA can do it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Remember only the current bracket nesting depth: 0, 1, 2 or 3.
2. `(` adds 1 to the depth; `)` subtracts 1.
3. `(` at depth 3 or `)` at depth 0 can never be repaired, so go to a dead state.
4. Accept only at depth 0.

```
   (     (     (     (
0 <-> 1 <-> 2 <-> 3 --> dead
|  )     )     )
+-- ) --> dead
```

That is 4 + 1 = 5 states, and all are pairwise distinguishable. The general lesson: bounded counting is regular; unbounded is not.

lessons.title: Nondeterministic paths and acceptance
lessons.summary: An NFA accepts when at least one path consumes the complete input and accepts.
lessons.body:
Try to build a DFA for "binary strings whose third symbol from the end is 1". It is awkward. As you read, you do not know which symbol will turn out to be third from the end, so the machine has to remember the last three symbols at all times. That needs 8 states.

Now imagine a machine allowed to **guess**. It reads along, and at some 1 it guesses "this is the one", then checks that exactly two more symbols follow. If any guess works out, the string is accepted. That machine needs 4 states and is obvious to design.

That is a **nondeterministic finite automaton** (NFA). The surprise, proved by Rabin and Scott in 1959, is that guessing adds no power: every NFA has an equivalent DFA. What it can add is **conciseness**, sometimes exponentially so.

## The definition

An NFA is described by the same five ingredients as a DFA (states, alphabet, transition function, start state, accepting states). Only the transition function changes: instead of naming one next state, it names a whole set of possible next states, and it may also move without reading anything.

```formula reference
DFA:  δ : Q × Σ → Q
NFA:  δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → P(Q)
δ(1, a) = ∅
where
DFA, NFA: labels saying which kind of machine each line describes
δ: Greek delta: the transition function
Q: the finite set of automaton states
Σ: capital Greek sigma: the input alphabet
×: the Cartesian product: the set of all (state, symbol) pairs
∪: union: the set of everything in either set
{ε}: the set containing just ε, the empty string. Allowing it as a "symbol" means a move can be made without reading input
→: maps to: δ takes a pair from the left-hand set and returns one element of the right-hand set
P(Q): the power set of Q: the set of all subsets of Q, from the empty set up to Q itself. A machine with 3 states has 2³ = 8 subsets
a: an input symbol (from the example below)
1: state 1 of the example below
∅: the empty set, a set with no elements: here, no move at all
In words: a DFA's transition function returns exactly one state; an NFA's returns a set of states, which may hold several states, one, or none, and an NFA may also have moves labelled ε that read no input.
```

So from a state on a symbol, an NFA can have:

- **several** next states (a choice),
- **no** next state (that path dies),
- **ε-transitions**, moves taken without reading any input.

An NFA **accepts** a string if **at least one** path through the machine consumes the whole string and ends in an accepting state. Paths that die or end elsewhere do not matter.

## Example: strings ending in ab

Over the alphabet {a, b}:

```
   a,b
   +-+
   v |
--> (0) --a--> (1) --b--> ((2))
```

| State | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|
| → 0 | {0, 1} | {0} |
| 1 | ∅ | {2} |
| 2 (accept) | ∅ | ∅ |

In this table, a set in curly braces lists the possible next states, and ∅ (the empty set) means there is no move: that path dies.

State 0 loops on everything, waiting. On an a it can also guess "this a starts the final ab" and move to 1. From 1, a b reaches 2. If more input follows, the path from 2 dies, which is fine; another path stayed in 0.

## Two ways to think about nondeterminism

1. **Guessing.** The machine magically picks the right move every time. If any sequence of choices leads to acceptance, it accepts. This is the view that makes NFAs easy to design.
2. **Parallel copies.** At each choice the machine clones itself. All clones run in lockstep. Accept if any clone consumes the full input and ends in an accepting state. This is the view that tells you how to **run** an NFA.

For efficient simulation, merge all copies at the same state and input position: keep the set of possible states, rather than one clone per path.

Trace `baab` through the NFA above:

```
start      {0}
read b ->  {0}
read a ->  {0, 1}
read a ->  {0, 1}
read b ->  {0, 2}   contains 2: accept
```

## Key takeaways
- An NFA accepts when at least one path consumes the complete input and accepts.
- Merge paths at the same state and input position when simulating.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)

2. Paths that die or end elsewhere are ignored.
3. Here one path qualifies, so the answer is accept.

lessons.title: Epsilon closure and free transitions
lessons.summary: Epsilon closure includes the starting states and every state reachable without consuming input.
lessons.body:
## ε-transitions and ε-closure

An ε-transition lets the machine change state for free. They make it easy to glue machines together: "do this OR that" becomes a start state with ε-arrows into two sub-machines.

The **ε-closure** of a set of states is that set plus everything reachable from it using only ε-arrows (zero or more of them). When simulating, you take the closure at the start and after every symbol.

Following zero arrows is allowed, so closure always includes the original states. Follow the arrows in their direction and keep going until no new states appear; an arrow labelled with a real symbol is excluded.

Example: accept strings of a's whose length is divisible by 2 **or** by 3.

Accept the input if either cycle returns to its accepting position. The empty string qualifies because both cycles start there.

```
      ε           a
 (s) ---> ((p0)) <---> (p1)
  |
  |   ε          a        a
  +-----> ((r0)) ---> (r1) ---> (r2)
             ^                   |
             +-------- a --------+
```

The start state s has ε-arrows to a 2-cycle and a 3-cycle.

Before reading anything, the current set contains s, p0 and r0. Since p0 and r0 accept, the empty string is accepted.

After one a the set is {p1, r1}: reject. After two, {p0, r2}: accept. The accepted lengths are 0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, and so on.

## Key takeaways
- Epsilon closure includes every starting state and all states reachable without consuming input.
- Epsilon branches combine the divisible-by-two and divisible-by-three languages using existential acceptance.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)

questions.prompt: An NFA has these ε-transitions: 1 → 2, 2 → 3, 4 → 1. There is also an `a`-transition 1 → 4. What is ε-closure({1})?

options.explanation: Correct. From 1 follow ε to 2, then ε to 3. Nothing else is reachable using only ε-arrows.
The closure always includes the starting states themselves (zero ε-moves is allowed).
1 → 4 is labelled a, not ε, so it consumes input and is not part of the closure. 4 → 1 points the wrong way.
The closure is transitive: once at 2 you can keep following ε to 3.

questions.workedExample: Start with state 1 itself: zero free moves are allowed. Follow its epsilon arrow to 2, then the epsilon arrow from 2 to 3. The arrow to 4 needs an a, and the epsilon arrow from 4 points into 1, not out of it. The closure therefore contains 1, 2 and 3 only.

lessons.title: Implementing set-based NFA simulation
lessons.summary: Take epsilon closure initially and after each consumed symbol.
lessons.body:
In the preceding epsilon-NFA: s branches freely to p0 and r0, which are accepting. The p states form a two-step a-cycle and the r states a three-step a-cycle. Closure includes a state and all states reachable by free arrows; the simulator keeps this set for every input position.

## Simulating an NFA in Python

```python
def close(delta, S):
    # Copy so closure does not mutate
    # callers.
    S = set(S)
    todo = list(S)
    while todo:
        q = todo.pop()
        # Follow only free arrows.
        for r in delta.get((q, ""), ()):
            # Discover each state only once.
            if r not in S:
                # This guard terminates
                # epsilon cycles.
                S.add(r)
                todo.append(r)
    return S

def run_nfa(delta, start, accept, w):
    # Include free moves before any input.
    S = close(delta, {start})
    for c in w:
        T = set()
        for q in S:
            # Merge paths reaching the same
            # state.
            T |= delta.get((q, c), set())
        # Free moves also follow consumed
        # symbols.
        S = close(delta, T)
    # Any accepting complete path is enough.
    return bool(S & accept)
```

Here ε is the empty string `""`. Each step looks at every current state and every arrow out of it at most once, and there is one closure for the start plus one step per input symbol. That gives this cost:

```formula reference
T = O((n + 1) × (m + e))
T = O((n + 1) × m)   when e = O(m)
where
T: the running time of run_nfa, counted in basic steps
O( ): Big O: an upper bound on growth that ignores constant factors
n: the length of the input string, in symbols; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
m: the number of NFA states; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
e: the number of transitions (arrows) in the NFA; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
In words: the work is at most the input length plus one, times the size of the machine. When each state has a bounded number of arrows out of it, the number of arrows is proportional to the number of states, and the bound simplifies to input length plus one, times states.
```

In words, the simulator stores at most one copy of each machine state, however many paths lead there. Each input symbol may require examining the whole machine, but it never enumerates all paths. For a fixed machine, doubling a sufficiently long input roughly doubles this worst-case work bound. A larger machine can still be expensive.

Writing m for the number of states, it needs O(m) working memory beyond the stored automaton. A Thompson-style NFA has at most two outgoing arrows per state, so its edges cannot add a separate large factor. This is the mechanism behind input-linear set simulation; it is a bound on growth, not a stopwatch prediction.

## Key takeaways
- Take epsilon closure initially and after each consumed symbol.
- A visited set terminates epsilon cycles; bounded out-degree gives work linear in input length for a fixed machine.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)

lessons.title: Building reachable subset states
lessons.summary: Each DFA state represents a set of possible NFA states.
lessons.body:
## The subset construction

The earlier NFA simulator already runs a DFA in disguise. Its "state" at each moment is a set of NFA states, and there are only finitely many such sets. Store each reached set as one named DFA state. Reaching that same set later means the same future behaviour, so its computed transitions can be reused.

Start with the epsilon closure of the NFA start. On each symbol, move every member, merge the destinations, then take epsilon closure again. A set accepts if any member accepts. If every path dies, the empty set is a rejecting state that stays empty on further input. These rules determine exactly one next set per symbol.

The reference notation records those rules:

```formula reference
S₀ = E({q₀})
T = E( ⋃_{q ∈ S} δ(q, c) )
S ∈ F_D   if   S ∩ F ≠ ∅
|Q_D| ≤ 2^m
where
S₀: the start state of the new DFA
E: the ε-closure: a set of states plus everything reachable from it by ε-arrows alone
q₀: the start state of the NFA
S: one DFA state, which is a set of NFA states
q: one NFA state inside S
c: one input symbol
δ: the NFA's transition function: δ(q, c) is the set of states q can move to on c
⋃_{q ∈ S}: big union: gather the results for every q in S into a single set
∈: is an element of
T: the DFA state reached from S on symbol c
F: the NFA's accepting states
∩: intersection: the states in both sets
≠: is not equal to
∅: the empty set
F_D: the DFA's set of accepting states
Q_D: the DFA's set of states
| |: vertical bars around a set mean its cardinality: the number of elements
≤: is less than or equal to
m: the number of NFA states; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
2^m: 2 to the power m: how many subsets a set of m states has
In words: start from the closure of the NFA's start state; on each symbol, move every member and take closure again. A set accepts if it contains any accepting state. Each original state may be present or absent, so the number of possible sets grows exponentially with the NFA's state count.
```

As a procedure:

1. Make the closure of the NFA's start state the DFA start state.
2. For each unprocessed DFA state and each symbol, compute the next set with the rule above. Add it if it is new.
3. Mark a DFA state accepting if it contains any NFA accepting state.
4. Stop when no new sets appear. Only build sets you can actually reach.

This is also called the **powerset construction**.

### Worked example: ending in ab

Start with {0}.

| DFA state | on a | on b | Accept? |
|---|---|---|---|
| → {0} | {0, 1} | {0} | no |
| {0, 1} | {0, 1} | {0, 2} | no |
| {0, 2} | {0, 1} | {0} | yes |

Only 3 of the eight (two to the power three) possible subsets are reachable. Rename them and you have an ordinary DFA:

| DFA state | Meaning | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|---|
| → A = {0} | no progress | B | A |
| B = {0, 1} | just saw a | B | C |
| C = {0, 2} (accept) | just saw ab | B | A |

### Worked example: the ε-NFA

For "length divisible by 2 or 3", the reachable subsets are {s, p0, r0}, {p1, r1}, {p0, r2}, {p1, r0}, {p0, r1}, {p1, r2} and {p0, r0}. That is 7 DFA states: the start, then six sets that track the length's remainder after dividing by 2 and its remainder after dividing by 3, together. The start and {p0, r0} turn out to be equivalent, so the minimal DFA has 6 states: one per remainder of the length after dividing by 6.

## Key takeaways
- Each DFA state represents a set of possible NFA states.
- A subset accepts if any member accepts; the empty subset is a dead state when reachable.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)


Curly braces list a set of possible next states, and - means no move. How many DFA states do you get?

options.explanation: Three is the size of the *minimal DFA*. The construction itself produces one more, because {0,1,2} and {0,2} are separate sets.
eight (two to the power three) is the upper bound. Only reachable subsets are built, and here only four are reachable.
No empty set is reached, because state 0 is always present (it loops on both symbols).
