| {0,1,2} | {0,1,2} | {0,2} |
| {0,2} | {0,1,2} | {0,2} |

Four sets. The last two both contain 2, so both accept, and both go to accepting sets on every symbol. They are equivalent, so minimisation would merge them into one "seen aa" state, giving 3.

questions.prompt: This ε-NFA recognises `a*b*`: state 0 loops on a, has an ε-arrow to 1, and state 1 loops on b and is accepting. Running the full subset construction (and counting ∅ if it is reached), how many DFA states result?

options.explanation: This forgets the dead state. From {1}, an `a` has nowhere to go, giving ∅, which must be a state in a complete DFA.
Correct: {0, 1} (start, accept), {1} (accept, b's only now) and ∅ (dead, after an a following a b).
All four subsets of {0, 1} are possible in principle, but {0} on its own is never reached: ε-closure always adds 1 whenever 0 is present.
One state cannot reject `ba`. The machine must remember whether a b has been seen.

questions.workedExample: The initial epsilon closure contains both 0 and 1, so it accepts empty input. An a keeps that set; a b leaves only state 1. From state 1, another b stays there but an a kills every path. The resulting empty set stays empty forever. These are three reachable states: both states, only 1, and the empty dead state.

lessons.title: Why determinisation can grow exponentially
lessons.summary: An NFA with m states has at most two to the power m subset states.
lessons.body:
## The exponential blow-up

Back to "the n-th symbol from the end is 1", where n is a fixed positive whole number such as 3. The NFA has one looping start state, one state for the guess on 1, then one state for each of the n − 1 "any symbol" steps that must follow. The subset construction produces:

| n | NFA states | DFA states |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 3 | 4 |
| 3 | 4 | 8 |
| 4 | 5 | 16 |
| 6 | 7 | 64 |

The pattern in the table, in symbols:

```formula essential
m = n + 1
d = 2^n = 2^{m − 1}
where
n: which position from the end must be 1 (n = 3 means third from the end); a positive integer
m: the number of NFA states; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
d: the number of states in the minimal DFA
2^n: 2 to the power n: the number of different bit strings of length n
In words: the NFA grows by one state each time n goes up by one, but the DFA doubles. For n = 6 the NFA has 7 states and the DFA has 2^6 = 64.
```

These DFAs are already minimal DFAs; you cannot do better. The reason is that the DFA must remember the last n symbols. Take two different strings u and v of length n. They differ at some position, say u has 1 and v has 0 at position i, counting from the left. Append i − 1 more symbols: now that position is n-th from the end, so one string is accepted and the other is not. So all two to the power n strings of length n need different states.

For example, with n set to 3, take u as `110` and v as `100`. They differ at position 2, so append one symbol, say `0`: `1100` has 1 third from the end (accept) and `1000` has 0 there (reject).

> [!warning] Worst case is real
> The general subset bound is exponential in the number of NFA states, and this family comes close to it. Full determinisation can be manageable for a given workload, but engines that build full DFAs ahead of time must guard against patterns like `(a|b)*a(a|b){20}`, which needs over a million states.

The practical consequence:

The general subset bound allows every combination of present or absent NFA states. In the position-from-end family, each extra remembered bit doubles the required DFA states. The regex `(a|b)*a(a|b){20}` therefore needs about 2.1 million states in its minimal DFA: a compact pattern can require a huge deterministic representation.

## Key takeaways
- An NFA with m states has at most two to the power m subset states.
- The n-th-from-end family has pairwise distinguishable length-n prefixes and needs exponentially many DFA states.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)

questions.prompt: An NFA has only a small number of states. Why might converting it to a DFA still use much more memory?

options.text: A DFA stores a separate copy of every input string
options.explanation: A DFA stores finite state, not its entire input history.

options.text: Every NFA transition must become a loop
options.explanation: Determinisation does not impose that transition structure.

options.text: Different reachable subsets become distinct DFA states
options.explanation: Correct. Many combinations of active NFA states may be reachable, even though each combination is small.

options.text: Determinisation adds unbounded counters
options.explanation: The result remains finite-state; the issue is the number of states.

questions.workedExample: The NFA simulator holds one set at a time. A full DFA stores a state and transitions for every reachable set. Each NFA state can be present or absent in a subset, so the space of possible subsets grows exponentially. Some NFAs reach very few of them; others force a large expansion.

questions.prompt: A DFA checks whether the tenth symbol from the end is 1. Why can it not remember only the total number of 1s in its recent input?

options.text: All inputs with the same count must be accepted
options.explanation: Position, not just count, determines this language.

options.text: It needs to remember all earlier symbols forever
options.explanation: Only a fixed recent window matters; the required memory is large but finite.

options.text: A DFA cannot remember any symbols
options.explanation: A state can encode a bounded window of symbols.

options.text: The order of recent bits determines future answers
options.explanation: Correct. Appending a suitable suffix can move a differing bit into the tenth-from-end position.

questions.workedExample: Two recent windows may contain the same number of 1s in different positions. Choose a position where they differ and append enough symbols to make that position tenth from the end. Exactly one resulting input accepts. The original windows therefore need different states, explaining the exponential family without calculating its size.

questions.prompt: For the language L of strings whose third symbol from the end is 1, the strings `110` and `100` must reach different DFA states. Which suffix z shows this, meaning exactly one of `110z` and `100z` is in L?

options.text: The empty suffix
options.explanation: Both `110` and `100` have 1 as their third-from-last symbol, so both are in L. ε does not separate them.

options.text: The suffix `00`
options.explanation: `11000` and `10000` both have 0 third from the end, so both are rejected. Too long a suffix pushes the difference out of the window.

options.text: The suffix `0`
options.explanation: Correct. `1100` has third-from-last 1 (accept); `1000` has 0 there (reject).

options.text: No suffix works; the two strings are equivalent
options.explanation: They differ in the middle position, and one extra symbol slides that position into third-from-last.

questions.workedExample: The two prefixes differ in their middle position. Append one symbol so that this differing bit becomes third from the end. With suffix 0, the strings are 1100 (accept) and 1000 (reject). With no suffix both accept; with suffix 00 both reject because the differing position has moved too far left. One continuation with different verdicts is enough to prove that two prefixes need distinct DFA states.

lessons.title: Lazy determinisation and model trade-offs
lessons.summary: Caching reached subsets can give table lookups without constructing every subset first.
lessons.body:
The subset construction represents an NFA by reachable sets of states. A set accepts whenever it contains an accepting NFA state; this existential rule is why complementing an NFA requires care.

## Why both models matter

- **NFAs are easy to build.** Union, concatenation and star are almost trivial with ε-arrows. That is why the regex-to-automaton construction (the following Thompson-construction units) produces an NFA.
- **DFAs are fast to run.** One table lookup per symbol, no sets.
- **Practical engines mix the two.** RE2 and Rust's `regex` do a **lazy subset construction**: they build DFA states on demand during matching and cache them. If the cache gets too big, they flush it or fall back to NFA simulation. You get DFA speed on typical inputs without paying the exponential cost up front.

In this comparison, m is the number of NFA states and e is the number of transitions (arrows).

| | NFA simulation | Full DFA |
|---|---|---|
| Build cost | O(m) for a Thompson-style NFA | potentially exponential, including transition computation |
| Time per symbol | O(m) for bounded out-degree | O(1) with a precomputed transition table |
| Memory | O(m + e), including transitions | O(2ᵐ) states; transition storage also depends on alphabet size |

## Pitfalls

- **Forgetting ε-closure.** Take the closure of the start state and after every step. Missing it makes ε-arrows invisible, and strings are wrongly rejected.
- **Complementing an NFA by swapping F.** This does not work. An NFA accepts if *some* path accepts, so after swapping, a string with one accepting and one rejecting path is accepted by both machines. Determinise first, then swap.
- **Treating nondeterminism as randomness.** An NFA does not flip coins. It accepts if an accepting path *exists*. It is an existence statement, like the "certificate" view of NP you will meet later.

## Key takeaways
- Caching reached subsets can give table lookups without constructing every subset first.
- Cache limits control memory; nondeterministic acceptance cannot be complemented by swapping accepting states.

## Further reading
- [MIT: nondeterminism and closure properties](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)
- [Rabin and Scott: finite automata (1959)](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~coquand/AUTOMATA/rs.pdf)
- [Russ Cox: matching in the wild](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html)

questions.prompt: A colleague wants an NFA for the complement of the language of an NFA N (every string N rejects), so they take N and swap accepting and non-accepting states. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: This can fail when some string has both an accepting and a non-accepting path in N
options.explanation: True. After the swap the non-accepting path becomes accepting, so the string is accepted by both N and the "complement".

options.text: It is safe if you first determinise N, make the DFA total, and then swap
options.explanation: True. A total DFA has exactly one run per string, so swapping F flips every answer.

options.text: It always works, because NFAs and DFAs recognise the same languages
options.explanation: Equal power does not mean every DFA trick works on NFAs. Complement by swapping depends on there being exactly one run.

options.text: Strings whose paths all die are mishandled too
options.explanation: True. They are rejected before and after the swap, because no path survives to reach any state.

questions.workedExample:
Take N to recognise "ends in ab" and take w as `ab`.

```
paths on "ab":
0 -a-> 0 -b-> 0   ends in 0
0 -a-> 1 -b-> 2   ends in 2
```

1. In N, the second path accepts.
2. Swap F: now 0 and 1 accept. The first path ends in 0, so `ab` is accepted again.
3. A correct complement would reject `ab`.

Fix: subset construction, add the empty-set dead state if needed, then swap. Regular languages are closed under complement, but the proof goes through the DFA.

questions.prompt: For a Thompson-style NFA with bounded out-degree, a regex engine uses a **lazy** subset construction, building DFA states only when the input reaches them and caching them. Which statements are true? Select all that apply. Write m for the number of NFA states and n for the input length. Assume expected O(1) cache lookup, O(m) work per uncached transition and bounded bookkeeping per step; only this single search is being analysed.

options.text: It avoids building DFA states that the input never reaches
options.explanation: True. Only subsets actually visited are computed.

options.text: A transition already in the cache can be followed by a table lookup
options.explanation: True for the assumed table-based cache. The transition-cache reuse fraction depends on the pattern, input and memory budget; no universal typical reuse measurement is implied.

options.text: It removes the exponential worst case entirely, so the cache can be unbounded
options.explanation: False. An adversarial input can still visit very many distinct subsets. Engines such as RE2 bound the cache and clear it or fall back to NFA simulation when it fills.

options.text: Its worst-case time stays linear in the input for a fixed pattern
options.explanation: True. Even when each new state has to be built, building one costs O(m), so total time is O(n · m).

questions.workedExample:
1. Each step either finds the next state in the cache (O(1)) or computes it from the NFA (O(m)).
2. So the worst case is O(n · m), same as NFA simulation, under the stated implementation assumptions. If most transitions are cached, most input steps use a lookup.
3. Memory is the risk: the number of distinct subsets visited can grow huge. RE2 keeps a fixed memory budget; when the cache fills it clears it and, if that keeps happening, it falls back to a slower matcher.
4. So lazy construction controls the blow-up in practice; it does not abolish it in theory.

link.title: Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast — Russ Cox

lessons.title: Formal regex languages and their limits
lessons.summary: Formal regexes combine empty language, empty string and symbols using union, concatenation and star.
lessons.body:
A tool such as grep -E can compile (a|b)*abb and scan input using the resulting matcher. Throughput depends on the tool, data, hardware and I/O. Between the pattern and the scan is a compiler. It parses the regex into a tree, turns the tree into an automaton, and runs the automaton over the text.

A standard first step of that compiler is **Thompson's construction**, published by Ken Thompson in 1968. It is short enough to write from memory, it produces an NFA linear in the size of the regex, and every piece of it is one of the three operations that define regular expressions.

## What a regular expression is, formally

Strip away the syntax sugar and a regular expression (regex) starts with three building blocks: no possible string, the empty string, or one alphabet symbol. Combine them by choosing either expression, joining one after another, or repeating zero or more times. These operations describe a language without prescribing a particular matching algorithm.

The formal notation is available as a reference:

```formula reference
L(∅) = ∅
L(ε) = {ε}
L(a) = {a}   for a ∈ Σ
L(R|S) = L(R) ∪ L(S)
L(R · S) = { x · y : x ∈ L(R), y ∈ L(S) }
L(R*) = {ε} ∪ L(R) ∪ L(R · R) ∪ …
where
L( ): the language of a regex: the set of strings it matches
∅: the empty set. As a regex it matches nothing at all
ε: Greek epsilon: the empty string. As a regex it matches only the empty string
{ }: the set of the items listed inside
a: any single symbol of the alphabet
Σ: capital Greek sigma: the input alphabet
∈: is an element of
R, S: any two smaller regular expressions
|: union (alternation): match R or S
∪: set union: every string in either set
·: concatenation: one thing straight after another. In regex syntax it is written by placing R and S side by side, as RS
x, y: a string matched by R and a string matched by S
*: the Kleene star: zero or more copies of R, one after another
…: and so on, with three, four, … copies
In words: the only building blocks are "nothing", "the empty string" and single symbols; the only ways to combine them are "either", "one then the other" and "repeat any number of times, including zero".
```

For example:

`a|b` chooses one symbol; `ab` requires a followed by b; `a*` allows any number of a characters, including none.

Read the basic syntax this way. R and S stand for smaller regular expressions; the empty string is written ε and the empty language ∅.

| Regex | Language |
|---|---|
| ∅ | no strings at all |
| ε | just the empty string |
| One alphabet symbol | just that one-symbol string |
| R \| S | strings matched by either expression |
| RS | a string from R followed by a string from S |
| R* | zero or more successive strings from R |

Everything else in everyday regex syntax is shorthand, as long as it stays regular:

- `R+` is `RR*`.
- `R?` is `R|ε`.
- `[a-c]` is `a|b|c`.
- `R{2,3}` is `RR|RRR`.
- In a formal wildcard notation, . can denote the union of the alphabet. Real regex engines commonly exclude newline unless a dot-all option is enabled.

General backreferences can express non-regular languages. The pattern (a+)b\1 matches some a's, a b, then exactly the same text as the first group again:

This pattern requires equally long a-runs on the two sides of b, with no upper bound. A finite automaton cannot remember an arbitrary first run accurately enough to compare the second.

Some individual backreference patterns are still regular: (a+)\1 matches positive even-length runs of a, equivalent to (aa)+. Engines such as RE2 reject the feature syntactically rather than proving regularity separately for each pattern.

Precedence, highest first: star, then concatenation, then union. So `ab|c*` means `(ab)|(c*)`, not `a(b|c)*`.

### Kleene's theorem

Stephen Kleene proved in 1956 that regular expressions and finite automata describe exactly the same languages:

- Every regex has an NFA (and hence a DFA) recognising its language. Thompson's construction is one proof.
- Every DFA has an equivalent regex. State elimination, in its later dedicated unit, is one proof.

That equivalence is why the languages are called *regular*: the regex view and the machine view are two descriptions of one class.

## Key takeaways
- Formal regexes combine empty language, empty string and symbols using union, concatenation and star.
- General backreferences can describe non-regular languages, although individual backreference patterns may be regular.

## Further reading
- [Russ Cox: simple and fast regular-expression matching](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html)
- [MIT: regexes to finite automata](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)

questions.prompt: Using standard regex precedence, which string does the whole regex `ab|c*` match?

options.text: `abc`
options.explanation: This reads the regex as `ab(c*)` or `a(b|c)*`. Union has the lowest regex precedence, so the regex is `(ab)|(c*)`, and `abc` is neither `ab` nor a run of c's.

options.text: `cc`
options.explanation: Correct. The regex is `(ab)|(c*)`; `cc` matches the right-hand side.

options.text: `ac`
options.explanation: This would need `a(b|c)`. Concatenation binds tighter than `|`, so `a` and `b` stick together.

options.text: `abcc`
options.explanation: The regex would have to be `ab(c*)` for this. Here the star applies only to `c`, and union separates `ab` from `c*`.

questions.workedExample:
Precedence, highest first: `*`, then concatenation, then `|`.

1. Star binds to the single symbol before it: `c*`.
2. Concatenation joins `a` and `b`: `ab`.
3. Union last: `(ab)|(c*)`.

So the language is {ab, ε, c, cc, ccc, ...}, where ε is the empty string (zero c's). Python agrees: `re.fullmatch("ab|c*", "cc")` matches and `"abc"` does not.

questions.prompt: Which of these regexes match exactly the same strings as `a+`? Select all that apply. Here ε is formal empty-string notation, not a character the engine matches.

options.text: `aa*`
options.explanation: Equivalent. One a, then any number more. This is the textbook definition of R+ as RR*.

options.text: `a*a`
options.explanation: Equivalent. Any number of a's followed by one more is still "one or more".
Not equivalent: `a*` also matches the empty string, which `a+` does not.
Not equivalent: choosing ε for the first part leaves `a*`, which matches the empty string.
Equivalent: brackets around a single symbol change nothing, so this is `aa*`.

questions.workedExample:
Check the boundary case, ε, and the general case.

| Regex | ε? | aaa? |
|---|---|---|
| `aa*` | no | yes |
| `a*a` | no | yes |
| `a*` | yes | yes |
| `(a\|ε)a*` | yes | yes |
| `a(a)*` | no | yes |

`a+` rejects ε and accepts every positive count, and the three equivalent expressions each describe exactly a positive run of a. These two test strings alone would not prove equivalence for an arbitrary regex; checking runs of zero through eight a characters is additional finite evidence.

questions.prompt: An automaton-based engine compiles patterns with Thompson's construction. Which of these can it support without leaving the regular languages? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Yes. It expands to `aa(a(a(a)?)?)?` or similar: finitely many copies.
Yes. A class is a union of symbols (one arrow with a range label in practice), and `+` is RR*.

options.text: General backreferences, including (a+)b\1
options.explanation: No. This particular pattern describes a run of a's, a b, then an equally long run of a's (at least one a each side), a non-regular language. By contrast (a+)\1 alone is regular, equivalent to (aa)+; the feature is rejected by these engines regardless.
Yes. ε is a base case, and union and star are basic operators. The NFA has an ε-cycle, which set simulation handles.

questions.workedExample:
Ask whether each feature reduces to ∅ (the empty set), ε (the empty string), symbols, union, concatenation and star.

| Feature | Reduces? |
|---|---|
| `{2,5}` | yes, by expansion |
| `[a-z]` | yes, a union |
| `+` | yes, RR* |
| `\1` | no |
| ε inside `*` | yes |

General backreferences exceed finite-automaton expressiveness, though some specific patterns using them remain regular. RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex reject the unsupported syntax rather than analyze such special cases.

lessons.title: Composing Thompson fragments
lessons.summary: Each fragment has one entry and one accepting exit.
lessons.body:
## Thompson's construction

The idea is structural induction. Build a small **NFA fragment** for each part of the regex, then glue fragments together. Every fragment keeps two promises:

1. It has exactly one **start state**, with no arrows coming in.
2. It has exactly one **accepting state**, with no arrows going out.

Those promises make gluing safe, because you never accidentally create a path into the middle of another fragment.

### Base case: a single symbol

```
--> (s) --a--> (f)
```

For the empty-string regex ε (Greek epsilon), use an ε-arrow, which reads no input, instead of a. For the empty-set regex ∅, which matches nothing, use two states and no arrow.

### Concatenation RS

Link R's accept state to S's start with an ε-arrow. R's accept stops being accepting.

```
--> [R: r0 ... r1] -ε-> [S: s0 ... s1]
```

The new fragment starts at r0 and accepts at s1.

### Union R|S

Add a new start with ε-arrows into both fragments and a new accept with ε-arrows out of both.

```
         ε                   ε
     +-----> (r0) ~R~> (r1) -----+
     |                           v
--> (s)                         (f)
     |   ε                   ε   ^
     +-----> (s0) ~S~> (s1) -----+
```

### Star R*

Add a new start and accept. From the new start you can skip R entirely or enter it. From R's accept you can loop back or leave.

```
                 ε (repeat)
            +-------------+
            v             |
--> (s) -ε-> (r0) ~R~> (r1) -ε-> (f)
     |                            ^
     +------------- ε ------------+
                 (skip)
```

`R+` is the same without the skip arrow. `R?` is the same without the repeat arrow.

### How big is the result?

The useful size guarantee is that every added part of the expression contributes only bounded extra structure.

Each symbol, empty-string or empty-language base case creates two states. Union and star each add two more, while concatenation adds an arrow. Each piece therefore adds only a bounded amount of machine structure: the construction grows linearly with the expanded expression.

For `(a|b)*abb`, this version builds 14 states. Each state has at most two outgoing arrows. Counted repetitions must be expanded before applying the linear-size claim: a short written count can describe many copies.

> [!note] Textbook variant
> Many textbooks, including the Dragon Book (Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman), merge R's accept state with S's start state during concatenation instead of adding an ε-arrow. That saves one state per concatenation. Both versions accept the same language.

## Parsing first: postfix

Building fragments needs a stack, and stacks work best on **postfix** notation. Two steps convert `(a|b)*abb`:

1. Insert an explicit regex-concatenation operator `.` wherever two items sit next to each other: `(a|b)*.a.b.b`.
2. Run the shunting-yard algorithm with regex precedence `*` > `.` > `|`: the result is `ab|*a.b.b.`.

Read the postfix left to right. A symbol pushes a new fragment. `*` pops one fragment and pushes its star. `.` and `|` pop two and push the combination.

## Key takeaways
- Each fragment has one entry and one accepting exit.
- Union and star add two states in this version; concatenation joins fragments with an epsilon arrow.

## Further reading
- [Russ Cox: simple and fast regular-expression matching](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html)
- [MIT: regexes to finite automata](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)

questions.prompt: A compiler concatenates two Thompson fragments using an epsilon arrow from the first exit to the second entry. Which change is necessary?

options.text: Keep both exits accepting
options.explanation: That would accept after the first fragment without matching the second.

options.text: Add a choice that skips the second fragment
options.explanation: Concatenation requires both fragments in order.

options.text: Use the first entry and only the second exit as the combined endpoints
options.explanation: Correct. The first exit becomes an internal state, joined to the second entry.

options.text: Reverse every arrow in the first fragment
options.explanation: Reversal would change the recognised strings.

questions.workedExample: A path must finish the first expression before entering the second. The connecting epsilon arrow consumes no extra input. Only reaching the second exit after the full input accepts the combined fragment; no new states are needed in this construction.

questions.prompt: In Thompson's fragment for R*, which arrow makes the empty string accepted even when R itself cannot match ε?

options.text: The ε-arrow from R's accept state back to R's start
options.explanation: That is the repeat arrow. It only matters after R has matched at least once.

options.text: The ε-arrow from the new start directly to the new accept
options.explanation: Correct. This "skip" arrow means zero copies of R are allowed, which is exactly ε.

options.text: The ε-arrow from the new start into R's start
options.explanation: This one enters R. To reach the accept state from there you must match R at least once.

options.text: None; ε is accepted only if R accepts ε
options.explanation: Zero repetitions are always allowed in a star, so R* always contains ε. That is what the skip arrow encodes.

questions.workedExample:
The star fragment adds four ε-arrows:

```
new start -> R start   (enter)
new start -> new accept (skip)
R accept  -> R start    (repeat)
R accept  -> new accept (leave)
```

On empty input, ε-closure of the new start includes the new accept via "skip", so ε is accepted. Remove the skip arrow and you have R+, which is RR*.

questions.prompt: You insert explicit concatenation dots into `a(b|c)*` and convert it to postfix with regex precedence `*` > `.` > `|`. What is the postfix?

options.explanation: Correct. `a`, then the group `bc|`, starred, then concatenated with `a`.
This applies the star to `c` alone. The star follows the closing bracket, so it applies to the whole group `b|c`.
This is `(ab|c)*`: it concatenates a and b before the union. The bracket puts `b|c` together first.
Postfix places every operator after its operands; this is still infix.

questions.workedExample:
1. Insert dots: `a.(b|c)*`.
2. Output `a`. Push `.`.
3. Inside the brackets output `b`, push `|`, output `c`. At `)` pop `|`: so far `abc|`.
4. `*` applies to the group just output: `abc|*`.
5. End of input: pop `.`: `abc|*.`.

Evaluating with a stack: push a; push b; push c; `|` combines b, c; `*` stars it; `.` joins a with it.

questions.prompt: An engine expands counted repetition into separate Thompson fragments. Why can a short pattern such as `(a|b){50000}` still exceed a compilation budget?

options.text: The engine stores just one fragment regardless of the count
options.explanation: Under the stated implementation it creates a separate copy for each repetition.

options.text: Every such pattern requires an exponentially large NFA
options.explanation: Expansion is linear in the expanded count; exponential determinisation is a different risk.

options.text: The written count describes many copies of the fragment
options.explanation: Correct. Source-text length does not bound the expanded machine size by a small constant factor.

options.text: Epsilon arrows consume the input during compilation

lessons.title: A postfix compiler and its resulting DFA
lessons.summary: This postfix compiler combines fragments without changing their accepted language.
lessons.body:
## Thompson's construction in Python

This compact compiler accepts validated postfix expressions of plain characters and the operators ., | and *. It omits parsing, escaping, character classes and explicit ε/∅ tokens. Its global state accumulates across calls; reset delta and n before comparing independent machine sizes.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

delta = defaultdict(set)  # (q, c) -> set
n = 0

def new():
    global n
    # Allocate a fresh state for each
    # fragment.
    n += 1
    return n - 1

def arc(a, c, b):
    delta[(a, c)].add(b)

def build(postfix):
    st = []   # stack of (start, accept)
    for c in postfix:
        if c == ".":
            s2, e2 = st.pop()
            s1, e1 = st.pop()
            # Concatenate without consuming
            # input.
            arc(e1, "", s2)
            st.append((s1, e2))
        elif c == "|":
            s2, e2 = st.pop()
            s1, e1 = st.pop()
            s, e = new(), new()
            # Branch into either
            # alternative.
            arc(s, "", s1); arc(s, "", s2)
            arc(e1, "", e); arc(e2, "", e)
            st.append((s, e))
        elif c == "*":
            s1, e1 = st.pop()
            s, e = new(), new()
            # Enter the body or skip zero
            # copies.
            arc(s, "", s1); arc(s, "", e)
            # Repeat the body or leave the
            # star.
            arc(e1, "", s1); arc(e1, "", e)
            st.append((s, e))
        else:                 # a symbol
            s, e = new(), new()
            arc(s, c, e)
            st.append((s, e))
    if len(st) != 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid postfix")
    return st.pop()

start, acc = build("ab|*a.b.b.")
# Five symbols, union and star: 14 states.
print(n)  # 14
```

The result plugs into `run_nfa` from the NFA simulator unit. `run_nfa(delta, start, {acc}, "babb")` is `True` and `"abba"` gives `False`: the expression requires the suffix abb. Testing a finite collection of strings can catch implementation mistakes; the fragment construction explains correctness for every input.

The important invariant is the fragment endpoint pair: each operator replaces its operands with a fragment for the combined expression.

## Worked example: (a|b)*abb to a DFA

Here is the classic Dragon Book version of the NFA, with concatenation states merged, so it has 11 states numbered 0 to 10:

```
0 -ε-> 1, 7
1 -ε-> 2, 4
2 -a-> 3      4 -b-> 5
3 -ε-> 6      5 -ε-> 6
6 -ε-> 1, 7
7 -a-> 8 -b-> 9 -b-> 10 (accept)
```

States 0 to 7 implement `(a|b)*`, including its exit at 7: 1 to 6 is the union, and 0, 6 → 1 and the arrows to 7 are the star. States 7 to 10 spell abb.

Now apply the subset construction. The start state is the ε-closure of state 0: everything reachable from 0 by ε-arrows alone.

Before any input, state 0 can reach 1 and 7 for free; state 1 can also reach 2 and 4. The initial subset therefore contains 0, 1, 2, 4 and 7. States 2, 4 and 7 are ready to consume a symbol.

| DFA | NFA states | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|---|
| → A | {0,1,2,4,7} | B | C |
| B | {1,2,3,4,6,7,8} | B | D |
| C | {1,2,4,5,6,7} | B | C |
| D | {1,2,4,5,6,7,9} | B | E |
| E (accept) | {1,2,4,5,6,7,10} | B | C |

Five DFA states from 11 NFA states. Read them as "how much of abb have I just seen": A and C mean none, B means a, D means ab, E means abb. A and C behave identically, so the minimal DFA (the minimisation units) has 4 states.

## Key takeaways
- This postfix compiler combines fragments without changing their accepted language.
- Subset construction can leave equivalent DFA states to merge later.

lessons.title: Turning an automaton back into a regex
lessons.summary: Eliminating a state preserves routes through it by concatenating entry, starred loop and exit labels.
lessons.body:
## The other direction: automaton to regex

To show every DFA has a regex, use **state elimination**:

1. Add a new start state with an ε-arrow to the old start, and a new single accept state with ε-arrows from the old accepting states.
2. Allow arrows to be labelled with regexes, not just symbols.
3. Remove the other states one by one. When you remove a state, replace every two-step path through it with a direct arrow whose label is given by the rule below, and union it with any existing direct arrow.
4. When only the new start and accept remain, the label between them is the regex.

The rule for step 3, when removing state q:

```formula essential
R_{pr}′ = R_{pq} · (R_{qq})* · R_{qr}
          | R_{pr}
where
q: the state being removed
p: a state with an arrow into q
r: a state with an arrow out of q
R_{pq}: the regex label on the arrow from p to q
R_{qq}: the label on q's self-loop (use ∅, the empty language, if there is none; its star matches ε)
R_{qr}: the label on the arrow from q to r
R_{pr}: the label already on the direct arrow from p to r (use ∅, the empty set, if there is none)
R_{pr}′: the new label on the direct arrow from p to r
·: concatenation: one part straight after the other
*: the Kleene star: zero or more repetitions
|: union (alternation): either side
In words: to get from p to r without q, you can go into q, loop round q any number of times, and come out to r, or you can take the direct arrow that was already there.
```

For the "even number of 1s" DFA from the DFA units (E loops on 0, 1 goes to O, O loops on 0, 1 goes back to E), eliminate O. The arrow into O is `1`, O's loop is `0` and the arrow out is `1`, so the path E → O → E becomes `10*1`. With E's own `0` loop the answer is `(0|10*1)*`.

Regexes produced this way can be exponentially longer than the DFA, and different elimination orders give different (equivalent) regexes. That is why tools go regex → automaton all the time and rarely the other way.

## Key takeaways
- Eliminating a state preserves routes through it by concatenating entry, starred loop and exit labels.
- Union preserves any existing direct route; the final regex may be much larger than the original DFA.

## Further reading
- [MIT: the regular pumping lemma and automata to regexes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec3-1/)

options.explanation: This drops q's self-loop. The path through q can go round the loop any number of times, so it must include `b*`.

options.text: `ab*c`

options.text: `ab*c|d`

This allows any order and any mix of the labels, which accepts many strings with no path in the automaton.

Alternation keeps both, giving `ab*c|d`. Forgetting the star loses repeated loops; forgetting d loses an existing route.

Fails on `0` and on `101`: this forces pairs of identical symbols, which is a much smaller language.
Correct. Leading 0s, then blocks that each contain exactly two 1s with any 0s after each. Every even-1s string splits this way.

Why it works: split an even-1s string before each odd-numbered 1. The prefix before the first 1 is `0*`; each block is a 1, some 0s, a 1, some 0s. Brute force over all strings up to length 10 agrees with the DFA.

lessons.title: Compiler choices and regex pitfalls
lessons.summary: Counted repetition can make a compact pattern compile into a large machine.
lessons.body:
The earlier construction builds epsilon-NFA fragments with one entry and one exit. Here we examine implementation choices and the boundary cases those fragments must handle.

## Where this shows up

- **lex and flex** compile token patterns into an NFA in this way, then determinise it ahead of time into a table-driven DFA. GNU grep may select DFA, fixed-string search or other matching strategies depending on options and pattern features.
- **RE2, Go's `regexp` and Rust's `regex`** compile into an NFA-like program of instructions (match a byte, split into two matching threads, jump) that is Thompson's NFA in a different notation. Russ Cox's articles show this "Pike VM" view.
- **Alternatives** exist. The Glushkov (or position) automaton has no ε-arrows and one state per symbol occurrence plus a start, which suits bit-parallel matching. **Brzozowski derivatives** build a DFA directly from the regex by repeatedly asking "what is left to match after reading this symbol?"

## Pitfalls

- **Precedence bugs.** `^ab|cd$` means `(^ab)|(cd$)`, not `^(ab|cd)$`. Many real validation bugs come from this.
- **Counted repetition is expansion.** `(a|b){1000}` becomes a thousand copies of the fragment, and `x{1,1000}` likewise. RE2 limits counted repetitions for this reason: its syntax rejects `{n}` when n exceeds 1000. Other engines have different limits and representations.
- **Star of something that matches the empty string.** `(a*)*` is legal, but the NFA has ε-cycles. Set simulation handles that fine because ε-closure visits each state once. A naive recursive backtracker without a zero-progress guard may loop; practical engines commonly detect empty repetitions, although other patterns can still cause excessive backtracking.

## Key takeaways
- Counted repetition can make a compact pattern compile into a large machine.
- Visited-state epsilon closure terminates even when nested stars introduce epsilon cycles.

## Further reading
- [Russ Cox: simple and fast regular-expression matching](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html)
- [MIT: regexes to finite automata](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)

questions.prompt: The Thompson NFA for `(a*)*` contains a cycle made entirely of ε-arrows. What happens when the set-of-states simulator from the NFA units runs it on `aaa`?

options.text: It loops forever computing the ε-closure
options.explanation: The closure uses a visited set: a state is added once and never re-expanded, so cycles terminate.

options.text: It terminates and accepts, in time linear in the input
options.explanation: Correct. Each ε-closure visits each state at most once, so every step is bounded by the NFA size.

options.text: It rejects, because ε-cycles make the NFA invalid
options.explanation: ε-cycles are legal and arise naturally from nested stars. The language is still a*.

options.text: It accepts, but takes time exponential in the input length
options.explanation: Exponential time is what a naive backtracking matcher can suffer on nested regex quantifiers. Set simulation never explores paths separately.

questions.workedExample:
1. `(a*)*` has the same language as `a*`, so `aaa` should be accepted.
2. The inner and outer stars create ε-arrows that form a loop.
3. The closure algorithm adds a state to the current set only if it is not already there, so it visits each state at most once: O(m) per step, where m is the number of NFA states.
4. Three steps of O(m) work each: linear.

A backtracking matcher, by contrast, can try many ways to split the input between the nested stars, and without protection it can even loop on the ε-cycle.

lessons.title: Why a long accepting run contains a loop
lessons.summary: The first pumping-length symbols visit more states than a DFA has.
lessons.body:
The DFA units claimed that no DFA recognises "equal numbers of a's and b's" or "balanced brackets". Claiming is easy. How do you **prove** that no DFA exists, out of the infinitely many you could build?

You cannot try them all. Instead you find a property that every regular language has, then show your language lacks it. The most famous such property is the **pumping lemma for regular languages**. It comes from one observation: a machine with p states that reads a string of length p or more must visit some state twice.

## The pigeonhole idea

Count state visits, including the start. Repeated visits count separately: the run does not gain new states when it loops.

Reading as many symbols as the DFA has states visits one extra state, because the start counts too. Some visit must repeat an earlier state. This already happens within that initial portion of the run.

This is the **pigeonhole principle**: put more than p pigeons into p holes and some hole holds two. It also tells you where the repeat happens. The first p symbols already give p + 1 visits, so some state repeats within the first p symbols.

For example, a 3-state DFA reading 5 symbols visits 6 states, so at least one of its 3 states appears twice, and the first repeat comes within the first 3 symbols.

Look at what happens between the two visits. The machine read some non-empty chunk and came back to where it was. So it is in an **automaton loop**:

```
          y
        +---+
        v   |
--> ... (q) +  ... --> accept
   x         z
```

Cut the string into three pieces around the loop:

```formula essential
s = x · y · z
δ̂(q₀, x) = q
δ̂(q, y) = q
δ̂(q, z) ∈ F
x · y^i · z ∈ L   for all i ≥ 0
where
s: the accepted string
x: the part read before first reaching the repeated state
y: the part read going round the loop, from q back to q; it is not empty
z: the rest of the string, read after the loop
·: concatenation: one string straight after another
q₀: the start state
q: the state that is visited twice
δ̂: "delta hat": δ̂(state, string) is the state you end in after reading the whole string from that state
∈: is an element of
F: the set of accepting states
L: the language the DFA recognises
y^i: i copies of y in a row; y^0 is the empty string, y^2 = y · y
i: how many times you go round the loop, 0, 1, 2, …
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: x leads to q, y goes from q back to q, and z leads from q to acceptance. Because y returns to q, the machine cannot tell how many times it went round, so repeating y, or deleting it, leaves a string the machine still accepts.
```

Skip the loop, follow it once or follow it repeatedly: after the unchanged suffix, every run ends in the same state. If one is accepted, they all are.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An extra lap
> On a walking route, a lap returns you to the same junction before you continue to your destination.
>
> **How it maps:** The junction is the repeated DFA state, the lap is the non-empty pumped piece, and the remaining route is the unchanged suffix. Taking zero or several laps still lets you follow that suffix.
>
> **Where it stops:** A physical walk may track elapsed time or tiredness. A DFA stores only its current state, so completing the loop leaves no extra memory of how often it happened.

### A concrete loop

Take the 3-state "divisible by 3" DFA from the DFA units and the string `1111` (15). The run is:

```
state:  0  1  0  1  0
read:     1  1  1  1
```

State 0 repeats after `11`.

The loop reads `11`. Skip it and the remaining input is `11`; take it once and the input is `1111`; take it twice and the input is `111111`. Each run returns to the same state before reading the final `11`, so all three strings are accepted.

The state path is enough to explain why all repetitions work; converting each binary string to a number adds no new justification.

## Key takeaways
- The first pumping-length symbols visit more states than a DFA has.
- A repeated state gives a non-empty loop that can be deleted or repeated.

## Further reading
- [MIT: the regular pumping lemma and automata to regexes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec3-1/)

lessons.title: The pumping lemma and adversarial choices
lessons.summary: A non-regularity proof must handle every pumping length and every legal split.
lessons.body:
## The lemma

> [!note] Pumping lemma for regular languages
> If a language is regular, there is a number, its **pumping length**, such that every string in the language at least that long can be cut into three pieces: a non-empty middle piece that lies within the first pumping-length symbols, and that can be repeated any number of times, or deleted, without leaving the language.

In symbols:

```formula essential
L ∈ REG   ⟹   ∃ p ≥ 1 such that
∀ s ∈ L with |s| ≥ p,
∃ x, y, z with s = x · y · z and:
  1.  |y| ≥ 1
  2.  |x · y| ≤ p
  3.  x · y^i · z ∈ L   for all i ≥ 0
where
L: the language
REG: the class of regular languages, those recognised by some DFA
⟹: implies: if the left side is true, the right side is true
∃: there exists: at least one such thing can be found
∀: for all: whichever one you pick
p: the pumping length, a whole number at least 1
s: any string in L
x, y, z: three pieces of s; y is the pumped piece
·: concatenation: one string straight after another
| |: vertical bars around a string mean its length
∈: is an element of
≥: is greater than or equal to
≤: is less than or equal to
y^i: i copies of y in a row; y^0 is the empty string
i: how many copies of y to use, 0, 1, 2, …
In words: if L is regular, then any long enough string in L has a non-empty piece near its start that can be repeated or deleted while staying in L.
```

For any DFA recognising L, p can be taken to be its number of states. Condition 2 holds because the repeat happens within the first p symbols. Note that zero copies (deleting y) are allowed, and is often the most useful choice.

For example, with the 3-state divisible-by-3 DFA a pumping length of 3 works, and the earlier loop-unit split of `1111` has a loop piece of length 2, lying inside the first 3 symbols.

## Using it: proof by contradiction

The lemma is a statement "if regular, then pumpable". To show L is **not** regular, show that L is not pumpable: then it cannot be regular, a **proof by contradiction**. The quantifiers ("for every", "there exists") matter, so it helps to see the proof as a game against an adversary who claims L is regular:

The order of choices matters: whatever pumping length is proposed, choose a sufficiently long member of the language. Then, for every permitted split of that string, show that some number of repetitions leaves the language. The repetition count may depend on the split.

As a game:

1. **Pumping adversary** picks the pumping length. You don't know it, so treat it as a variable.
2. **You** pick a long enough string in L. Choose wisely; this is the creative step.
3. **Pumping adversary** picks any legal split. You must beat **every** possible split.
4. **You** pick the number of copies of the middle piece and show the result is not in L.

If you can always win, L is not regular.

## Key takeaways
- A non-regularity proof must handle every pumping length and every legal split.
- Choose the witness after the pumping length and the repetition count after the split.

## Further reading
- [MIT: the regular pumping lemma and automata to regexes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec3-1/)

options.explanation: Flaw. The adversary chooses p. The proof must work for any p, so use p a’s followed by p b’s as the witness.

options.text: Choosing a specific y instead of handling every legal split
options.explanation: Flaw. The adversary chooses the split. Showing one bad split proves nothing.

options.text: Using two copies rather than zero copies
options.explanation: Not a flaw. Any single i that breaks membership is enough, and two copies works here.

options.text: Choosing a member of L at least as long as the pumping length
options.explanation: Not a flaw. This is required: s must be in L and at least p long.

Choose a run of a characters as long as the proposed pumping length, followed by the same number of b characters. Every permitted pumped piece lies inside the first run; doubling any such non-empty piece makes the counts unequal. Either deletion or duplication can supply the contradiction here.

## Example 1: a's followed by the same number of b's

The language is every string of some a's followed by exactly as many b's. To expose the missing memory, put all the a characters first. Any legal loop near the beginning then changes the a count without touching the b count.

```formula essential
L = { a^n b^n : n ≥ 0 }
s = a^p b^p,   |s| = 2p ≥ p
y = a^k,   1 ≤ k ≤ p
x · y^2 · z = a^{p + k} b^p ∉ L
where
L: the language
a, b: the two symbols
a^n: n copies of a in a row, so a^3 = aaa; a^0 is the empty string
n: any whole number 0 or more
p: the pumping length, whatever the adversary chose; a positive integer measured in input symbols
s: the string we choose: p a's then p b's
| |: the length of a string
x, y, z: the adversary's split of s
y^2: y twice
k: the length of y; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
·: concatenation
∈, ∉: is, and is not, an element of
≥, ≤: greater than or equal to, less than or equal to
In words: choose p a's followed by p b's. Any legal y lies in the first p symbols, which are all a's, so y is a block of k a's. Repeating it gives more a's than b's, which is not in L.
```

Step by step:

1. Let p be the pumping length.
2. Choose s as p a's then p b's. It is in L and has length 2p, which is at least p.
3. Any split has x and y within the first p symbols. Those are all a's, so y is k a's, with k at least 1.
4. Pump with two copies of y: the result has p + k a's and only p b's, so it is not in L.

Contradiction, so L is not regular. For instance, if the adversary chose pumping length 3 and pumped piece `aa`, the string `aaabbb` pumps to `aaaaabbb`, with 5 a's and 3 b's.

The choice of s did the work. Putting all the a's in the first p symbols forced y to contain only a's, so we did not need to consider cases.

> [!tip] Why condition 2 is your friend
> Condition 2 pins the pumped piece inside the first p characters. Pick a string whose first p characters are "all the same kind", and the adversary has no room to manoeuvre.

## Example 2: palindromes

A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards, like `abba` or `aabaa`. Let L be the palindromes over {a, b}.

Choose a palindrome with a long a-run, one b, and the same a-run again. Make each run as long as the proposed pumping length. Every legal pumped piece lies entirely in the first run. Deleting it shortens only that side, so b is no longer in the middle and the result is not a palindrome.

For example, deleting the first a from `aabaa` gives `abaa`, which no longer reads the same backwards. The general argument works regardless of how long the legal piece is.

The same template works for the language of "doubled" strings, a string followed by an exact copy of itself:

Choose a block consisting of a pumping-length run of a characters followed by b, then write that entire block twice. This is a doubled string, and its initial run forces the pumped piece to contain only a characters.

Again the pumped piece lies entirely in the first a-run. Deleting it leaves exactly two b characters and the final character is b. If the result had two identical halves, each half would contain one b and end at that b. The two a-runs would then have to be equal, but only the first was shortened. No choice of a new halfway point repairs this mismatch.

## Key takeaways
- Uniform first symbols force the pumped piece into one run.
- Deleting or repeating one side breaks equal counts, palindromes and the chosen doubled-string witness.

lessons.title: Arithmetic witnesses and pumping down
lessons.summary: Square-length witnesses pump strictly between consecutive squares.
lessons.body:
## Example 3: perfect squares

Consider strings of a characters whose length is a **perfect square** (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …). The useful observation is that gaps between squares grow. Choose a square large enough that duplicating any allowed pumped piece increases the length without reaching the next square. The following short inequality is the proof of that gap, rather than a calculation to memorise.

```formula essential
s = a^{p²},   |s| = p²
y = a^k,   1 ≤ k ≤ p
|x · y^2 · z| = p² + k
p² < p² + k ≤ p² + p < (p + 1)²
where
s: the string we choose: p² a's
a: the only symbol
p: the pumping length; a positive integer measured in input symbols
p²: p squared, p × p
| |: the length of a string
x, y, z: the adversary's split
y^2: y twice, so one extra copy
k: the length of y; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
·: concatenation
<: is less than
≤: is less than or equal to (the first comparison makes k at least 1)
(p + 1)²: the next perfect square after p², equal to p² + 2p + 1
In words: one extra copy of y adds between 1 and p symbols, which lands strictly between p² and the next square, so the new length is not a square.
```

So p² + k lies strictly between two consecutive squares and is not a square. Contradiction. With pumping length 3: lengths 10, 11 or 12, all between 9 and 16.

## Example 4: more a's than b's

Let L be the strings of a's then b's with more a's than b's. Pumping up only adds more a's, which keeps the string in L. So pump **down**.

Choose a string with exactly one more a than b, with the b-run as long as the proposed pumping length. Any legal pumped piece contains only a characters. Removing it loses at least the one-character lead, while leaving every b in place. The result no longer has more a characters than b characters.

For example, with pumping length three, `aaaabbb` loses at least one a and becomes, say, `aaabbb`. Equality already violates the strict requirement for more a characters.

The lesson: try both directions. Different languages break under different numbers of copies.

## A prime-length witness

The prime-length language is another arithmetic example. Choose a prime length at least two larger than the positive pumping length; arbitrarily large primes exist. Once the adversary chooses a legal non-empty piece, choose enough repetitions to make the resulting length a product of two integers greater than one. Such a product is composite, so it leaves the prime-length language. The choice is allowed to depend on the piece length; it must work for every permitted piece.

Here is the optional factorisation that supplies that repetition count:

```formula reference
q ≥ p + 2     1 ≤ k ≤ p
i = q − k
(q − k) + ik = (q − k)(1 + k)
q − k ≥ 2     1 + k ≥ 2
where
q: a prime integer, the chosen input length in symbols
p: the positive integer pumping length in symbols
k: the integer length of the non-empty pumped piece in symbols
i: the non-negative integer number of copies of that piece
≥, ≤: greater than or equal to, less than or equal to
In words: choose the number of copies to equal the length left after deleting the original piece. The resulting total is that remaining length multiplied by one more than the piece length; both factors are at least two, so the new length is composite.
```

For example, prime length seven and a pumped substring of length two give five copies and a new length of fifteen. The argument works for every legal pumped-substring length, rather than relying on this one example.

## Key takeaways
- Square-length witnesses pump strictly between consecutive squares.
- For a strict count inequality, deleting the pumped piece can break membership when repeating it cannot.

## Further reading

lessons.title: Closure proofs and the limits of pumping
lessons.summary: Intersecting with a regular language can isolate a known non-regular matching-count language.
lessons.body:
## Shortcuts with closure properties

Regular languages are closed under intersection, union, complement and more: combining regular languages with these operations always gives a regular language. That gives a second tool.

Let L be the strings over {a, b} with equally many a's and b's. The same p a's then p b's witness proves non-regularity directly. Closure gives another proof:

```formula essential
L ∩ a*b* = { a^n b^n : n ≥ 0 }
where
a, b: the two input symbols
L: strings with equally many a's and b's
∩: intersection: the strings in both languages
a*b*: the regular language "any number of a's, then any number of b's"
*: the Kleene star: zero or more copies
a^n b^n: n a's followed by n b's
n: any whole number 0 or more
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: the strings with equal counts that also have all their a's before their b's are exactly the a's-then-equal-b's strings from Example 1.
```

1. Suppose L were regular.
2. a*b* is regular.
3. Then their intersection would be regular, because regular languages are closed under intersection.
4. But that intersection is the language from Example 1, which we proved is not regular.

Contradiction. Balanced brackets fall the same way: intersect with the regular language consisting of zero or more opening brackets followed by zero or more closing brackets, and you get n opening brackets followed by n closing ones, which is Example 1 in disguise.

## What it means in practice

- **Regex cannot parse nested structure.** HTML, JSON, arithmetic expressions and balanced brackets all contain Example 1-style matching. A true regex can handle a fixed maximum depth, but not arbitrary nesting. Use a parser (a pushdown automaton, next module).
- **Some engines go beyond regular.** Perl, PCRE and .NET support recursion or balancing groups and can match balanced brackets. These features go beyond formal regular expressions. Their performance depends on the engine and pattern; recognising balanced brackets itself can be done in linear time with a parser.
- **Counting has to be bounded.** "At most 3 levels of nesting" or "at most 255 characters long" is regular; "same number of opening and closing tags" is not.

## Pitfalls

- **The lemma does not prove regularity.** It is "regular implies pumpable", not the other way round. Some non-regular languages are pumpable; an example follows this list. The Myhill–Nerode theorem (in the later minimisation units) gives an exact test.
- **You do not choose the split.** A proof that says "let y be a" only handles one split. You must show every legal split fails.
- **You do not choose the pumping length.** Writing "let p be 5" proves nothing. Keep p symbolic.
- **Pick a long enough string.** A string shorter than the pumping length is outside the lemma's promise.
- **Finite languages are always regular**, so you cannot prove a finite language non-regular. Every finite language trivially satisfies the lemma, with a pumping length longer than its longest string.

The pumpable but non-regular example:

Consider ordered a-runs, b-runs and c-runs with this rule: either there are no a characters, or the b and c counts match. Every non-empty member can pump its first symbol: changing a positive a-run preserves matching b and c counts, while deleting its last a removes the comparison requirement. If there are no a characters, the rule allows any b and c counts. Thus pumping length one works.

Nevertheless, intersect with `ab*c*`, which requires exactly one a. The result must have equal b and c counts with no bound. That is non-regular: in a pumping proof, deleting a pumped piece containing the initial a removes the required a; otherwise repeating a piece of the initial b-run unbalances the counts. Passing the pumping test does not prove regularity.

## Key takeaways
- Intersecting with a regular language can isolate a known non-regular matching-count language.
- Pumpability is necessary for regularity but is not sufficient.

## Further reading
- [MIT: the regular pumping lemma and automata to regexes](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec3-1/)

lessons.title: Equivalent states and distinguishing suffixes
lessons.summary: Equivalent states agree on every possible continuation, including empty input.
lessons.body:
The subset construction and hand design both tend to produce DFAs with redundant states: two states that look different but behave identically on every possible future input. Merging them gives a smaller machine that accepts exactly the same language.

Do it until nothing more can be merged and you reach the **minimal DFA**. A remarkable fact: for each regular language over a fixed alphabet, the minimal complete DFA is unique up to renaming states. That makes it a canonical form for regular languages. Two regexes describe the same language exactly when their minimal complete DFAs agree up to a renaming that preserves the start state, transitions and accepting status, which turns "are these equivalent?" into a mechanical check.

## When are two states the same?

Two states are **equivalent states** if every possible future input gives the same verdict from both. They are **distinguishable states** if some input string (a **distinguishing suffix**) takes one to an accepting state and the other to a non-accepting state.

```formula reference
p ≡ q   iff   ∀ z ∈ Σ* :
  δ̂(p, z) ∈ F   ⟺   δ̂(q, z) ∈ F
where
p, q: two states of the same DFA
≡: is equivalent to
∀: for all
z: any input string, thought of as "the rest of the input"
Σ*: every finite string over the alphabet Σ, including the empty string ε
∈: is an element of
δ̂: "delta hat": δ̂(p, z) is the state reached by starting at p and reading all of z
F: the set of accepting states
⟺: holds exactly when: either both sides are true or both are false
In words: ("iff" means "if and only if".) Two states are equivalent when, for every possible remaining input, both accept or both reject. If even one string gets different verdicts, that string distinguishes them.
```

Two observations drive every algorithm:

1. An accepting and a non-accepting state are distinguished by the empty string: you are already there, and one accepts.
2. If two states move, on some symbol, to a pair of states already known to be distinguishable, then the two states are distinguishable too: by that symbol followed by the old distinguishing string.

If a symbol sends the two states to distinguishable successors, put that symbol before the suffix which separates the successors. That longer suffix now separates the original states too.

For example, in the following refinement unit’s worked example, A and D both move to B on `a`, but on `b` they move to A (rejecting) and E (accepting). The empty string distinguishes A from E, so `b` distinguishes A from D.

Equivalent states can be merged. Unreachable states can simply be deleted. A DFA with no unreachable states and no equivalent pairs is a minimal DFA.

## Key takeaways
- Equivalent states agree on every possible continuation, including empty input.
- A suffix distinguishing successors also distinguishes their predecessors when its input symbol is prepended.

## Further reading
- [Minimization of Automata — Berstel, Boasson, Carton and Fagnot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5318)

lessons.title: Partition refinement and table filling
lessons.summary: Remove unreachable states before counting the minimal machine.
lessons.body:
## Worked example

This DFA accepts strings over {a, b} that end in ab, but it was built carelessly:

| State | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|
| → A | B | A |
| B | D | C |
| C (accept) | D | A |
| D | B | E |
| E (accept) | B | A |
| F | C | F |

### Step 1: remove unreachable states

Search from A: A reaches B; B reaches D and C; D reaches E. Nothing reaches F, so delete it. Five states remain.

### Step 2: partition refinement (Moore's algorithm)

Start from the coarsest guess, two blocks: accepting and non-accepting. Then repeatedly split any block whose members disagree about which block they go to on some symbol.

Round 0:

The initial non-accepting block contains A, B and D. The accepting block contains C and E. They must remain separate because the empty continuation already distinguishes the two verdicts.

Round 1. For each state, note which block each transition lands in:

```
     on a   on b
A    N      N
B    N      Acc
D    N      Acc
C    N      N
E    N      N
```

A disagrees with B and D (its b goes to N, theirs to Acc), so split N into {A} and {B, D}. C and E agree, so they stay together.

```
{A}   {B, D}   {C, E}
```

Round 2. Recheck with the new blocks. B goes to D on a and C on b; D goes to B on a and E on b. Both land in ({B, D}, {C, E}), so they still agree. C and E both go to {B, D} on a and {A} on b. Nothing splits, so we have a **stable partition**.

The minimal DFA has 3 states:

| Block | Meaning | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|---|
| → {A} | no progress | {B,D} | {A} |
| {B,D} | just saw a | {B,D} | {C,E} |
| {C,E} (accept) | just saw ab | {B,D} | {A} |

That is the same machine the subset construction gave in the NFA units, as uniqueness promises.

### The same thing in Python

```python
def minimise(states, alpha, delta, accept):
    states = tuple(states)
    alpha = tuple(alpha)
    # start: split accepting / non-accepting
    part = {q: q in accept for q in states}
    while True:
        # Keep the block and all successor
        # blocks.
        sig = {q: (part[q],) + tuple(
                   part[delta[(q, c)]]
                   for c in alpha)
               for q in states}
        ids = {}
        # Equal signatures receive one new
        # block.
        new = {q: ids.setdefault(sig[q],
                                 len(ids))
               for q in states}
        old = len(set(part.values()))
        # Refinement cannot merge old
        # blocks.
        if len(ids) == old:
            return new   # stable: no split
        part = new
```

Each state's **refinement signature** is its current block plus the blocks it moves to. States with equal signatures stay together. When a round creates no new blocks, stop. On the example (with F removed) it returns `{A: 0, B: 1, C: 2, D: 1, E: 2}`: three blocks, B with D and C with E.

The DFA must be complete (every transition defined), so add a dead state first if needed. Remove unreachable states before calling this function. It returns state-to-block IDs; constructing the quotient transitions, start and accepting states is a separate step.

## The table-filling algorithm

The textbook alternative (Hopcroft and Ullman) works on pairs. Draw a triangle with one cell per pair of states.

1. Mark every pair where one is accepting and the other is not.
2. Repeat: mark a pair if, on some symbol, its two successors form a pair that is already marked (the rule below).
3. When a full pass marks nothing, every unmarked pair is equivalent.

Propagate a distinction backwards: if one symbol leads to a marked pair, mark the original pair. Prepending that symbol to the known distinguishing suffix explains why the new mark is justified.

For our five states:

```
    A    B    C    D
B   x1
C   x0   x0
D   x1   =    x0
E   x0   x0   =    x0
```

`x0` means marked in step 1 (different acceptance). `x1` means marked in the first pass: for (A, B), reading b gives (A, C), which is already marked. The two unmarked cells are (B, D) and (C, E), the same merges as before.

Table filling is easy to do by hand but takes O(n²) space for n states. It also tells you why each pair differs, which helps when debugging.

## Key takeaways
- Remove unreachable states before counting the minimal machine.
- Refinement splits acceptance blocks to a fixed point; table filling marks distinguishable pairs.

## Further reading
- [Minimization of Automata — Berstel, Boasson, Carton and Fagnot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5318)

lessons.title: Hopcroft and double reversal
lessons.summary: Smaller-half scheduling limits repeated transition work in Hopcroft refinement.
lessons.body:
Moore refinement repeatedly splits states by their successor blocks until the partition stops changing. Here we compare its cost with two other minimisation methods.

## How fast?

The running times below are written in Big O notation, in terms of two sizes of the DFA:

```formula reference
T_Moore = O(k n²)
T_Hopcroft = O(k n log_2(n))
where
T_Moore: the worst-case running time of Moore's partition refinement
T_Hopcroft: the worst-case running time of Hopcroft's algorithm
O( ): Big O: an upper bound on growth that ignores constant factors
n: the number of states in the DFA; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
k: the size of the alphabet (the number of different input symbols); an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
n²: n squared, n × n
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, so log_2(1024) = 10
In words: Moore's worst-case bound grows with the square of the state count and with the alphabet size. Hopcroft's bound grows with the state count times its slowly growing logarithm, again scaled by alphabet size. Careful scheduling limits repeated scanning.
```

The practical distinction is repeated work. Moore's method may rescan states over many rounds. Hopcroft schedules carefully chosen splitters so large blocks do not keep causing the same work. These bounds describe growth, not measured speed on a particular machine. Table filling with a dependency worklist has the same quadratic worst-case growth as Moore; repeated full passes can be slower.

**Hopcroft's algorithm** is the standard choice for large automata. Its worklist rule matters: if a split block is already pending, replace it with both pieces; otherwise schedule only the smaller piece. With reverse transition lists, each transition can be charged only logarithmically many times in the number of states: each newly scheduled smaller piece is at most half its previous block's size.

**Brzozowski's algorithm** is strange and elegant: reverse the automaton, determinise, reverse again, determinise again.

```flow
Reverse the automaton
Build reachable subset states
Reverse the result
Build reachable subset states again
```

Reversal flips every arrow and exchanges initial and accepting roles. Several initial states may result; represent them with a fresh start and epsilon arrows if a single start is required. Each determinisation keeps only reachable subsets.

The result is always the minimal DFA. Its worst case is exponential because each determinisation can blow up, but it can be fast in practice and works directly on NFAs.

## Key takeaways
- Smaller-half scheduling limits repeated transition work in Hopcroft refinement.
- Double reversal and reachable determinisation give a minimal DFA, with exponential worst-case intermediates.

## Further reading
- [Minimization of Automata — Berstel, Boasson, Carton and Fagnot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5318)

lessons.title: Myhill–Nerode and DFA lower bounds
lessons.summary: Two prefixes are language-equivalent when no continuation separates them.
lessons.body:
## The Myhill–Nerode theorem

Minimisation rests on a theorem that describes the minimal DFA without mentioning any machine at all.

For a language, call two strings **L-equivalent** if no suffix tells them apart:

```formula essential
x ≡_L y   iff   ∀ z ∈ Σ* :
  x · z ∈ L   ⟺   y · z ∈ L
where
x, y: two strings, thought of as "inputs read so far"
L: the language
≡_L: is L-equivalent to
∀: for all
z: any possible continuation (suffix)
Σ*: every finite string over the alphabet, including the empty string
·: concatenation: x followed by z
∈: is an element of
⟺: holds exactly when: both sides true, or both false
In words: ("iff" means "if and only if".) Two prefixes are L-equivalent when every possible ending puts both in L or both outside L. The strings sharing one verdict-pattern form an equivalence class.
```

For "strings ending in ab", `a` and `bba` are L-equivalent (both just saw a), while `a` and `b` are not: appending `b` gives `ab` in L and `bb` outside it.

> [!note] Myhill–Nerode theorem
> L is regular if and only if L-equivalence has finitely many classes. When it does, the number of classes equals the number of states in the minimal DFA.

The intuition: a DFA state is exactly "everything about the past that matters for the future". Strings that reach the same state of the minimal DFA are L-equivalent, and each class is one state.

### A second way to prove non-regularity

Myhill–Nerode is an exact test, unlike the pumping lemma for regular languages. To show L is not regular, find infinitely many strings that are pairwise distinguishable.

Take the language of n a's followed by n b's. The strings a, aa, aaa, ... are pairwise distinguishable:

Choose any two different positive lengths of initial a-run. Appending just enough b characters to match the first run accepts that prefix and rejects the other. This works for every pair, so no two different counts can share a state.

For example, `aa` and `aaa` are separated by `bb`: `aabb` is in L and `aaabb` is not. Infinitely many classes, so not regular. No case analysis about splits, no choice of how many copies to pump.

### Lower bounds on DFA size

It also gives tight lower bounds. In the NFA units, "the n-th symbol from the end is 1" needed two to the power n states, that is n copies of 2 multiplied together, where n is the position being checked. That was a Myhill–Nerode argument: the two to the power n strings of length n are pairwise distinguishable. For position 3 that is 8 strings, `000` to `111`, and 8 states.

## Key takeaways
- Two prefixes are language-equivalent when no continuation separates them.
- Infinitely many pairwise distinguishable prefixes prove non-regularity.

## Further reading
- [Minimization of Automata — Berstel, Boasson, Carton and Fagnot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5318)
- [Stanford CS103: nonregular languages](https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs103/cs103.1266/lectures/18/)

One for each two-bit ending (00, 01, 10, 11) overcounts. Endings 00 and 10 behave identically: what matters is just "the last symbol was 0".
Correct: "ends in 01", "ends in 0", and everything else (ε or ends in 1 but not 01). So the minimal DFA has 3 states.

options.text: Infinitely many, since L is infinite
options.explanation: An infinite language can have finitely many classes; that is exactly what regular means.

Group strings by what suffixes they need:

|---|---|---|---|
| ends 01 | `01` | no | yes |

| other | `11`, ε | no | no |

The three rows differ in some column, so the classes are distinct. These classes also form a closed transition system: on 0 every class goes to ends-0; on 1 ends-0 goes to ends-01 and the other classes go to other. Only ends-01 accepts, so all strings within each class have identical futures. There are exactly 3, and the minimal DFA has 3 states.

options.text: For palindromes, prefixes of any number of a’s then b are separated by appending the first prefix’s number of a’s
options.explanation: Valid. Append as many a’s as occur before the b in the first prefix. It becomes a palindrome; a prefix with any different number of a’s does not.

options.text: For a’s followed by equally many b’s, different lengths of initial a-runs are separated by a matching number of b’s
options.explanation: Valid. A suffix of i b’s completes a prefix of i a’s into the language but rejects any prefix with a different number of a’s.

options.text: a*b* has infinitely many a-prefixes, so it is not regular
options.explanation: Invalid. All a-only prefixes have the same allowed continuations in this language. Infinitely many prefixes do not help unless they are pairwise distinguishable.
