For palindromes, take different a-runs followed by b; an a-run matching the first prefix completes only that palindrome. For equal a-then-b counts, a matching b-run separates different initial a-runs. In `a*b*`, however, all a-only prefixes have the same future possibilities. In even-length strings only parity matters, so infinitely many prefixes still fall into two classes.

lessons.title: Minimal machines in practice
lessons.summary: A product search can find a shortest counterexample without fully minimising either DFA.
lessons.body:
A minimal complete DFA merges equivalent states after unreachable states have been removed. The Myhill–Nerode units explain why its states are determined by the language.

## What minimal DFAs are used for

- **Automaton equivalence testing.** To check `a(ba)*` against `(ab)*a`, build both minimal DFAs and compare. Both describe alternating strings that start and end with a, so they come out identical. In practice tools skip full minimisation and search the product automaton for a reachable pair (p, q) where exactly one accepts; the path to it is a counterexample. For a*b* versus (ab)*, a and b are both shortest counterexamples; alphabet traversal order determines which is returned.
- **Lexer generators.** Generators that emit a DFA as code or tables, such as re2c, minimise it first, which directly shrinks the generated scanner.
- **Hardware.** Fewer logical states may reduce storage or logic, but encoding and synthesis matter. The same binary bit count can cover several state counts, and next-state logic can become more complex.
- **Model checking and verification.** Verification tools minimise automata to shrink the state spaces they have to explore and store.
- **Learning automata.** Angluin's L* algorithm learns a minimal DFA using membership queries and equivalence queries that return counterexamples when a hypothesis is wrong. It is used to infer models of black-box network protocols and software.

## Pitfalls

- **Minimising an NFA is hard.** Uniqueness and these fast algorithms apply to DFAs. The decision problem of whether an equivalent NFA with at most a given number of states exists is PSPACE-complete, even when the input is a DFA. Minimum NFAs need not be unique.
- **Forgetting the dead state.** If your DFA is partial, add the dead state before refining, otherwise states that "fall off" on different symbols may be wrongly merged.
- **Forgetting unreachable states.** They do not change the language, but they inflate the count. Partition refinement on its own will not delete them.
- **Merging on one step.** Two states with identical rows and the same accepting status are equivalent, but states with different rows can still be equivalent (B and D in the earlier refinement example have different rows). Refinement has to run to a fixed point.

## Key takeaways
- A product search can find a shortest counterexample without fully minimising either DFA.
- Uniqueness and fast minimisation apply to complete DFAs over a fixed alphabet; minimum NFAs behave differently.

## Further reading
- [Minimization of Automata — Berstel, Boasson, Carton and Fagnot](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5318)

2. NFAs have no such unique minimal representation. The decision problem "is there an NFA with at most k states?" is PSPACE-complete.
3. DFA minimisation is efficient (O(k n log n) for n states and k symbols), which is why the minimal DFA is a practical canonical form for automaton equivalence tests.

lessons.title: Matching strategies and repeated paths
lessons.summary: Path enumeration can revisit the same state and input position through many decompositions.
lessons.body:
Two engines can recognise the same language while doing very different amounts of work. A path-enumerating backtracker can revisit the same state and input position exponentially many times; a set-based simulation merges those repeated situations.

## Matching strategies and guarantees

In the cost discussion, m is the compiled pattern size, including counted-repeat expansion, and n is the input length. Set simulation performs at most a machine-sized amount of work per input symbol, plus initialisation. The optional bound records that relationship:

```formula reference
W = O(m × (n + 1))
where
W: the total work of one search by set simulation, in basic steps
O( ): Big O: an upper bound on growth that ignores constant factors
m: the compiled pattern size: roughly the number of NFA states or instructions, including expansions such as counted repetition; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
n: the length of the input text, in characters; an integer count, non-negative unless a positive lower bound is stated
In words: set simulation does at most a pattern-sized amount of work per input character, plus one extra round at the start, so this upper bound grows linearly with input length for a fixed compiled pattern; it does not predict an exact time.
```

Set simulation limits each input step to work bounded by the compiled machine size. For a fixed pattern this gives input-linear growth. Changing the pattern size or repeatedly calling the search API changes the total workload.

| Strategy | Idea | Important limit |
|---|---|---|
| Unmemoized backtracking | Try choices depth-first and revisit alternatives after failure | Ambiguous patterns can take exponential time |
| Thompson/Pike simulation | Merge equivalent active states at each input position | Bounded-out-degree machines use O(m·(n + 1)) work |
| Lazy DFA | Caches sets of active states and their transitions | Full determinisation can require exponentially many states |

For a fixed pattern, m is a constant, so a documented O(m·n) single-search guarantee is linear in input size.

Production libraries combine strategies. Python re, Java's standard engine and default PCRE2 matching use backtracking; RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex provide input-linear single-search guarantees for their supported syntax. A bounded memoized backtracking implementation can also avoid repeated state/position work. Ruby 3.2 added memoization for many patterns; PCRE2 has a separate DFA-style API; GNU grep chooses methods according to options and syntax. Engine names alone do not specify every mode's behavior.

## How backtracking works

A backtracking engine walks the NFA **depth-first**. At every choice (an alternation, or "one more iteration or stop?"), it tries one option and remembers the other. If the path fails later, it returns to the most recent choice point and tries the alternative.

Here is the idea as code, run directly on a Thompson NFA like the one built in the Thompson-construction units:

```python
calls = 0

def bt(q, w, i):
    global calls
    # Count visits, including revisited
    # states.
    calls += 1
    if q == acc and i == len(w):
        return True
    # Try free moves before consuming a
    # symbol.
    for r in delta.get((q, ""), ()):
        if bt(r, w, i):
            return True
    if i < len(w):
        for r in delta.get((q, w[i]), ()):
            # This branch consumes exactly
            # one symbol.
            if bt(r, w, i + 1):
                return True
    return False
```

This teaching function requires a supplied delta and accepting state. It has no memoization, handling of excessive call nesting or epsilon-cycle guard; do not use it as a production matcher. A successful path may be found early, but other patterns can do extensive work before eventually succeeding. Failure may require exploring all remaining choices.

### Why it explodes

Consider full-string matching `(a+)+` against a run of n a's followed by one b (n at least 1), using an unoptimized path-enumerating backtracker.

The run of a's can be split among the inner `a+` iterations in many ways: for each of the gaps between neighbouring a's, choose whether to start a new inner iteration there.

Every gap between neighbouring a characters can either separate two inner repetitions or stay inside one. Adding another a adds a new independent cut-or-no-cut choice, doubling the number of decompositions. A matcher that retries each decomposition repeats work exponentially.

`aaaa` could be (aaaa), (a)(aaa), (aa)(aa), (a)(a)(aa), and so on: 8 splits in all. With 30 a's there are two to the power twenty-nine, over 500 million. Every split reaches the b and fails. The backtracker tries them all, because it does not remember that it has already been in this NFA state at this input position and failed.

That is the whole problem. The set simulation merges all those paths: it only asks *which states* are reachable after i characters, not *how*.

## Key takeaways
- Path enumeration can revisit the same state and input position through many decompositions.
- A fixed-pattern input-linear guarantee is different from a bound that also includes pattern size.

## Further reading
- [Russ Cox: simple and fast regular-expression matching](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html)
- [MIT: regexes to finite automata](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-404j-theory-of-computation-fall-2020/resources/mit18_404f20_lec2-1/)

lessons.title: Ambiguous patterns, growth and outages
lessons.summary: Nested repetition and overlapping alternatives can create exponentially many paths.
lessons.body:
A path-enumerating backtracker retries alternatives after a path fails. Here the input length counts the repeated a characters before the final failing symbol, unless stated otherwise.

## Growth without a timing claim

For a path-enumerating matcher without memoization or simplifying optimizations, (a|aa)* on a failing run has Fibonacci-many decompositions: the first part has length one or two.

The first repetition consumes either one a or two. Each choice leaves a shorter run with the same problem, so alternatives branch repeatedly. The decomposition counts begin 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8: each count combines the previous two. This is exponential growth even though it does not double with every character.

For example, four a characters can be consumed as four singles, two doubles, or one double with two singles in three different orders. These are different paths over the same text. Path counts explain potential repeated work; they are not exact CPU instruction counts or universal timing predictions.

## The danger patterns

Exponential blow-up needs **ambiguity**: several different paths through the pattern that consume the same text. Look for:

- **Nested regex quantifiers**: `(a+)+`, `(a*)*`, `(\w+\s?)*`.
- **Overlapping alternatives under a regex repetition operator**: `(a|a)*`, `(\w|\d)+`, `(.|\s)*`.
- **Adjacent repeated parts that can match the same characters**: `.*.*=`, `\d+\d+`. On their own these are usually polynomial, but repeated or nested inside another regex repetition operator they compound.

There is also a **polynomial** form, which is less dramatic per character but easier to trigger:

- An unoptimised search for `\s+$` on a run of spaces followed by x tries every space as a starting position, and from each start scans the remaining spaces before failing at the x.

The first starting position scans all the spaces. The next scans almost all of them, and so on. Doubling the run creates roughly twice as many starting positions, each with roughly twice as much scanning available: quadratic growth. Faster scanning at a single start does not remove the repeated-start cost.

Actual engine optimizations and constants determine runtime.

## Real outage

> [!example] Cloudflare, 2 July 2019
> A new web application firewall rule contained `.*(?:.*=.*)` inside a larger pattern. Deployed globally at once, it drove CPUs serving HTTP traffic to nearly 100% and took down Cloudflare's proxy and CDN for 27 minutes. Cloudflare's postmortem shows the simplified `.*.*=.*;` taking 5,353 steps to fail on `x=` followed by 20 x's. Among the follow-ups: switching the WAF to RE2 or Rust's regex engine, both documented as providing runtime guarantees.

The shared cause: a pattern that looked fine, an input nobody had tested, and a regex evaluated on a hot path.

## Key takeaways
- Nested repetition and overlapping alternatives can create exponentially many paths.
- Repeated-start searches may also have polynomial worst cases; failing almost-matches expose the work.

## Further reading
- [Cloudflare: details of the July 2019 outage](https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/)
- [Russ Cox: simple and fast matching](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html)

questions.prompt: An unoptimised search for `\s+$` tries each space as a new starting point in a long run of spaces followed by x. Why can the total work be quadratic?

options.text: Only the final character is examined
options.explanation: Each attempt first scans spaces before failing at x.

options.text: Many starts each rescan a long overlapping suffix
options.explanation: Correct. Longer input creates more starts and more scanning per start.

options.text: The engine has exponentially many nested repetitions
options.explanation: This example needs no nested repetition; repeated starts are enough for polynomial growth.

options.text: A single pass stores every substring
options.explanation: The work comes from revisiting text, not necessarily storing substrings.

questions.workedExample: At the first space, the attempt scans the whole run and fails at x. The next attempt repeats most of that work, then the next repeats slightly less. Summing the overlapping scans gives quadratic growth. A pattern can therefore be costly even without exponential ambiguity. Actual optimisations may change a particular implementation’s behaviour.

questions.prompt: In an anchored, path-enumerating backtracker without memoization or pattern simplification, which patterns have exponentially many ambiguous paths on a run of n a characters followed by !? Select all that apply. (two to the power n means n copies of 2 multiplied together.)

Exponential: each a can be matched by either branch, giving two to the power n paths.
Not exponential. At a fixed start, a single regex repetition operator scans and may backtrack through linearly many match lengths.
Exponential. Since `\s?` can match nothing, this behaves like `(\w+)*` on a run of letters: nested regex quantifiers.
Not exponential. Each iteration of the group must end at a space, so a run of letters can be split only one way.

Duplicate alternatives in (a|a)* allow two to the power n branch sequences. The single-run a+ and mandatory-separator rewrite do not have that exponential ambiguity. These are conceptual path counts, not measured timings; optimizations may collapse duplicate alternatives.

lessons.title: How automaton engines control repeated work
lessons.summary: Set simulation merges equivalent active states, while lazy DFAs cache reachable subsets.
lessons.body:
In this unit, m is the compiled pattern size and n is the input length. Bounds concern one search, with input and pattern measured in the chosen engine’s units.

## How automaton engines avoid it

RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex prevent unrestricted repeated exploration for their supported single searches. Implementations can combine several methods, including bounded memoized path exploration. The main ideas:

1. **Thompson NFA simulation** (the earlier NFA and Thompson-construction units): track the set of active states. O(m) per character, where m is the compiled pattern size.
2. **Pike VM**: the same, but each active matching state carries its capture-group positions, with a priority order so results match Perl's leftmost-first semantics.
3. **Lazy DFA**: cache subset-construction states as they are discovered. A cached transition can be followed with a table lookup; the transition reuse fraction is workload-dependent. RE2 bounds the cache's memory; if it fills too often, it falls back to the NFA.
4. **Literal prefilters**: scan for a required fixed string (say `ERROR` in `ERROR.*timeout`) with fast substring search, and only run the automaton near hits.

Go's documentation states the guarantee directly: matching is "guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input". Rust's says searches are worst case O(m · n), with m the pattern size and n the input length.

### The price

Features that are not regular, or are expensive to simulate, are left out:

- **Backreferences** like `(\w+) \1`. General backreferences can express non-regular languages, although individual backreference patterns can still be regular; `^(..+)\1+$` on a string of a's matches exactly when the length is composite. General backreferences cannot be implemented by ordinary finite automata. This does not mean every individual backreference pattern is slow or non-regular.
- **Lookaround** (`(?=...)`, `(?<=...)`) is unsupported in RE2, Go and Rust's `regex`. .NET's NonBacktracking mode also excludes lookarounds and backreferences.
- **Atomic groups and possessive quantifiers** can change which strings match. They have meaning beyond a particular execution algorithm: PCRE2’s DFA-style matcher supports them with documented semantics. RE2, Go and Rust regex omit this syntax.

Linear time is per search. Rust's documentation notes that iterating over **all** matches can be O(m · n²) in the worst case, where m is the compiled pattern size including counted-repeat expansion and n is the input length in bytes: up to n searches, each linear. And large patterns cost memory: counted repetition of a Unicode class, such as `\w{200}`, compiles to a big automaton, which is why these libraries enforce size limits on compiled patterns.

## Key takeaways
- Set simulation merges equivalent active states, while lazy DFAs cache reachable subsets.
- Supported syntax and per-search guarantees matter; iterating all matches can have a different bound.

## Further reading
- [Go regexp matching guarantee](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp)
- [Rust regex guarantees](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)
- [Russ Cox: matching in the wild](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html)

questions.prompt: Why does RE2 reject the pattern `(\w+) \1`?

options.text: It is a syntax error in every engine
options.explanation: Perl, PCRE, Python and Java all accept it. It is a deliberate omission in RE2.

options.text: This particular backreference pattern describes a non-regular language outside RE2’s supported syntax
options.explanation: Correct. Arbitrarily long word-copy matching here exceeds finite-automaton expressiveness. Not every pattern containing a backreference is non-regular.

options.text: RE2 does not support capture groups
options.explanation: RE2 supports captures through its Pike VM. It refuses only references back to them.

options.text: The pattern is vulnerable to ReDoS
options.explanation: RE2 accepts many regular patterns that would cause excessive backtracking elsewhere. It excludes backreference syntax; its matching guarantee does not remove all resource-exhaustion risks.

questions.workedExample:
1. A finite automaton can only remember a bounded amount.
2. `(\w+) \1` must remember an arbitrarily long word to compare it later, like ww from the pumping-lemma units, which is not regular.
3. Ordinary finite automata cannot recognize this language, and RE2 excludes this syntax. Lookaround is excluded too.

Fun fact: `^(..+)\1+$` on a string of a's matches exactly when the length is composite. This pattern recognises runs of a single repeated character with composite length, not primes; rejecting it does not by itself classify 0 and 1 as prime. A finite automaton cannot recognize the unbounded composite-length language.

questions.prompt: An automaton-based engine like RE2 builds a lazy DFA, caching states as it meets them. Write m for the compiled pattern size (roughly the number of NFA states) and n for the input length. What happens when an adversarial input makes it discover huge numbers of distinct DFA states?

options.text: It fails because its DFA cache grows without a bound
options.explanation: A bounded cache prevents unlimited DFA-cache growth. It does not guarantee that the entire application can never exhaust memory.

options.text: It falls back to unrestricted, unmemoized backtracking
options.explanation: That would lose the guarantee. Bounded memoized backtracking is a different technique that RE2 can use for suitable searches.

options.text: It clears the cache and, if that keeps happening, falls back to slower NFA simulation, staying linear time
options.explanation: Correct. Throughput drops, but the O(m · n) bound holds.

options.text: It precomputes the full DFA first to avoid this
options.explanation: Full determinisation can need 2ᵐ states (m copies of 2 multiplied together), which is exactly the blow-up the lazy approach exists to avoid.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each lazy-DFA state is a set of NFA states, computed on demand in O(m).
2. Cached transitions are cheap when reused; distinct-set count depends on the pattern and input.
3. An adversarial input can keep producing new sets. The cache reaches its configured capacity.
4. RE2 then flushes the cache and carries on; if it is flushing too often to be useful, it falls back to NFA simulation.
5. Worst case per character is still O(m), so the whole match stays linear in input length for a fixed compiled pattern.

lessons.title: Choosing engines and defending validators
lessons.summary: Removing ambiguity must preserve the intended full-match language and capture behaviour where needed.
lessons.body:
## Defences

1. **Use a linear-time engine for untrusted input or untrusted patterns.** Python has the `google-re2` bindings; Java has RE2/J; .NET 7+ has `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking`; V8 described an experimental linear engine and /l flag in a 2021 article; availability depends on runtime version and runtime command-line options, so this is not a portable JavaScript feature. Bound pattern size, compilation resources and input volume even with linear matching.
2. **Remove ambiguity.** `(a+)+` is just `a+`. `(\w+\s?)*` has the same full-match language as `(\w+\s)*\w*`, but in the second form every word must end at a space, so each string can be matched only one way. Captured-group results can differ. Unanchored searches also need separate complexity analysis.
3. **Use atomic groups or possessive quantifiers** where the engine has them. Python 3.11 added both: `(?>a+)+$` and `(a++)+$` eliminate that nested pattern’s repeated splitting because the inner group cannot give back characters. Atomicity does not make every surrounding search safe and can change accepted input.
4. **Bound the input.** Cap field lengths before matching. Reject overlong values rather than validating only a truncated prefix: truncation can hide an invalid suffix.
5. **Set timeouts** where supported: .NET's `Regex` accepts a match timeout. Python's `re` and Java's `java.util.regex` have none built in, so use a killable process or an execution boundary that actually stops the work on deadline. Timing out a waiting thread does not necessarily stop the underlying match.
6. **Test with failing inputs.** Long almost-matches (many a's then a wrong character) are what expose backtracking. Static analysers and fuzzers for ReDoS exist for several languages.
7. **Don't use regex for nested structure.** Formal regular expressions cannot recognise arbitrary nesting. Bounded nesting and richer engine features are different cases; use a suitable parser for general structured formats.

## Choosing an engine

- **Backtracking** is right when you need backreferences or lookaround, patterns are written by your own developers, and inputs are bounded. Check the chosen implementation, input-length caps and required features; developer-authored patterns can also be vulnerable.
- **Automaton-based** is right when patterns or inputs come from users (search boxes, WAF rules, application event log filters, user-supplied validation), when inputs are large (grep over gigabytes), or when predictable scaling matters. This still requires explicit caps on memory and execution time, plus workload testing.

## Key takeaways
- Removing ambiguity must preserve the intended full-match language and capture behaviour where needed.
- Combine suitable engines with bounded resources, failing-input tests and enforceable execution deadlines.

## Further reading
- [Python re: syntax and atomic groups](https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html)
- [RE2 supported syntax](https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax)
- [Rust regex guarantees](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)

questions.prompt: A developer "hardens" a validator by rewriting `(\w+\s?)*` as `\w+(\s\w+)*`. Tests pass on normal input. What has changed besides speed? Compare full-match acceptance, not capture contents.

options.text: Nothing: the two are equivalent
options.explanation: They are not. The original accepts the empty string and strings with a trailing space, e.g. `a b `; the rewrite rejects both.

options.text: The rewrite now rejects the empty string and a trailing space, which the original accepted
options.explanation: Correct. (\w+\s)*\w* preserves full-match acceptance, including empty and trailing-whitespace cases; captured groups can differ.

options.text: The rewrite accepts double spaces, which the original rejected
options.explanation: Neither accepts two spaces in a row: each `\s` must sit between word characters (or at the very end, in the original).

options.text: The rewrite is now vulnerable to ReDoS
options.explanation: The mandatory separator removes this nested ambiguity, but the rewrite accepts a different language. Do not infer a universal safety guarantee for every search mode.

questions.workedExample:
Compare on edge cases (full match):

| Input | original | rewrite | `(\w+\s)*\w*` |
|---|---|---|---|
| (empty) | yes | no | yes |
| `a b` | yes | yes | yes |
| `a b ` | yes | no | yes |

Removing ambiguity is the right idea, but a rewrite must keep the language. Brute-force over all strings of a and space up to length 9 supports the full-match equivalence on that finite set. The general argument groups each non-final word with its following whitespace; capture results are not claimed equivalent.

questions.prompt:
Python 3.11+ supports atomic groups. What do these print?

```python
import re
# Ordinary repetition can give back an
# a.
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"a*a", "aaa")))
# The atomic group cannot give one back.
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?>a*)a",
                        "aaa")))
```

options.text: `True` then `True`
options.explanation: The atomic group grabs all three a's and will not give one back, so the final `a` has nothing to match.

options.text: `False` then `True`
options.explanation: `a*a` matches `aaa` normally: `a*` backtracks one character so the last `a` can match.

options.text: `True` then `False`
options.explanation: Correct. Ordinary `a*` gives back an a; atomic `(?>a*)` cannot, so the second pattern can never match.

options.text: `False` then `False`
options.explanation: The ordinary pattern is fine: backtracking lets `a*` take two a's and `a` take the third.

questions.workedExample:
1. `a*a` on `aaa`: `a*` greedily takes 3, `a` fails, backtrack: `a*` takes 2, `a` matches the third. True.
2. `(?>a*)a`: the atomic group takes 3 a's and, once it exits, its choice is final. `a` has nothing left and the engine may not revisit the group. False.
3. This is how atomic groups remove this particular repeated-splitting problem: `(?>a+)+$` cannot try exponentially many splits. But they change what matches, so use them only where giving back characters could never help, such as `(?>a+)b`.

Possessive `a*+a` is the same as `(?>a*)a`.

questions.prompt: For which of these should you prefer an automaton-based engine (RE2, Go, Rust `regex`) over a backtracking one? Select all that apply.

options.text: A search service for application event logs where customers type their own patterns
options.explanation: Yes. Untrusted patterns are the classic case: one customer's `(a+)+$` must not stall the cluster. Also bound compiled pattern size and total work.

options.text: A web firewall applying thousands of rules to every HTTP request
options.explanation: Yes. Huge volume, attacker-controlled input and a hot path: Cloudflare's 2019 outage was exactly this.

options.text: An existing full-match operation requiring `(\w+)=\1` on explicitly bounded, vetted local input, without rewriting the operation
options.explanation: The listed engines reject backreferences. Use a suitably constrained supporting engine, or redesign as capture plus an ordinary equality check. Source files are not automatically trusted, especially from external contributions.

options.text: Scanning multi-gigabyte files for `ERROR.*timeout`
options.explanation: Yes. Linear time, literal prefilters and a lazy DFA make automaton engines (and grep) fast on huge inputs.

questions.workedExample: For untrusted or large workloads, documented scaling guarantees are useful alongside input, pattern and compilation budgets. RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex reject the listed backreference. A supporting engine or capture-and-compare redesign is needed. Lookaround is not exclusive to backtracking: PCRE2’s separate DFA-style matcher supports it.
